docs.title: Chapter 7: Pressure & Safety Relief Systems
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: State the difference between a pressure relief valve (PRV) and a pressure safety valve (PSV), and identify which API standard governs each
  • Understand: Explain the operating principle of a spring-loaded PRV and describe what happens during simmer, pop, and reseat
  • Apply: Determine the required relief capacity (SCFM or GPM) for a fire case and blocked outlet case given vessel and piping data
  • Analyze: Identify conditions that cause a PRV to chatter and explain the root cause
  • Evaluate: Compare the advantages of a pilot-operated relief valve (PORV) vs. a spring-loaded PRV for a high-pressure gas application with a narrow operating margin

docs.title: 7.1 Why Pressure Relief Exists
docs.text:
Every pressure vessel, heat exchanger, pump, and piping system has a maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP). If process upsets, control failures, or fire cases exceed the MAWP, the equipment fails — catastrophically in high-pressure service. Pressure relief devices are the last line of defense — a passive, automatic protection device that opens to vent excess pressure and reseats when pressure returns to normal.

Regulatory framework: - ASME Section VIII, Division 1: Design and construction of pressure vessels; mandates relief device installation - API 520 Part I: Sizing of pressure relieving devices - API 520 Part II: Installation of pressure relieving devices - API 521: Guide for pressure-relieving and depressuring systems (disposal) - API 526: Flanged steel pressure relief valves (standard orifice sizes) - OSHA PSM (29 CFR 1910.119): Process Safety Management — relief system documentation requirements

docs.title: 7.2 Spring-Loaded Pressure Relief Valves
docs.text: The spring-loaded PRV is the most common pressure relief device. A spring holds a disc against a nozzle seat. When inlet pressure overcomes spring force, the disc lifts, venting fluid until pressure drops and the spring reseats the disc.

docs.title: Key Terminology
docs.text: Term Definition Set pressure Pressure at which the PRV begins to open (pops) Overpressure Allowable pressure above set at full flow (typically 10% for process, 21% for fire case) Accumulation Maximum pressure above MAWP during a relief event Blowdown Pressure drop below set pressure before the PRV reseats Simmer Slight leakage/seepage just below set pressure — indicates valve is near opening Chatter Rapid opening and closing — destructive; occurs when PRV is oversized or inlet pressure drop is too high Back pressure Pressure on the outlet (discharge) side — affects set pressure in conventional PRVs

docs.title: PRV vs. PSV
docs.text: The terms are often used interchangeably, but: - PRV (Pressure Relief Valve): Opens proportionally to overpressure — primarily for liquid service where proportional flow is needed - PSV (Pressure Safety Valve): Opens with a "pop" action — required for compressible fluids (gas, steam) where the full area must be exposed quickly - Safety Relief Valve: Dual-purpose — can operate as either PRV or PSV; most process industry valves are this type

docs.title: API Orifice Sizes
docs.text:
API 526 standardizes relief valve orifice sizes by letter designation:

Orifice Area (in²) Common applications D 0.110 Small liquid lines E 0.196 Small vapor/gas F 0.307 Medium service G 0.503 Medium-large H 0.785 Large process J 1.287 Very large process K 1.838 Large steam L 2.853 Very large steam M 3.600 Largest standard

docs.title: 7.3 Sizing Pressure Relief Valves
docs.text: Relief valve sizing begins with identifying the governing relief case — the scenario requiring the largest relief capacity.

docs.title: Common Relief Cases
docs.text: Case Trigger Governing fluid Blocked outlet Downstream block valve closes while pump/compressor runs Liquid or vapor at pump/compressor rated flow Control valve fails open Upstream CV opens fully Maximum inlet flow Fire case External fire heats vessel liquid Vapor at heat input rate Cooling failure Cooling water loss — reaction exotherm Vapor at heat generation rate Power failure Pumps/compressors stop; control valves fail Depends on fail-safe action Tube rupture High-pressure shell fluid enters low-pressure tubes High-pressure fluid at exchanger differential

docs.title: Sizing for Vapor/Gas (API 520)
docs.text:
$$A = \frac{W}{C \cdot K_d \cdot P_1 \cdot K_b \cdot K_c} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{T \cdot Z}{M}}$$

Where: - W = required flow (lb/hr) - C = gas constant based on ratio of specific heats (k) - K_d = effective discharge coefficient (typically 0.975 for gas) - P_1 = relieving pressure (set + overpressure + atmospheric), psia - K_b = back pressure correction factor - K_c = combination correction (1.0 if no rupture disc) - T = relieving temperature (°R) - Z = compressibility factor - M = molecular weight

docs.title: Sizing for Liquid (API 520)
docs.text:
$$A = \frac{Q}{38.0 \cdot K_d \cdot K_w \cdot K_c \cdot K_v} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{G}{P_1 - P_2}}$$

Where Q = required flow (GPM), G = specific gravity, P₁ = set pressure (psia), P₂ = back pressure (psia).

docs.title: 7.4 Pilot-Operated Relief Valves (PORVs)
docs.text:
A pilot-operated relief valve uses process pressure to keep the main disc closed — the inlet pressure acts on a larger area on top of the disc than on the bottom, creating a net closing force. A small pilot valve senses inlet pressure and releases the top-loading when set pressure is reached, allowing the main disc to open fully.

Advantages over spring-loaded:

Advantage Explanation Tight shutoff near set pressure No simmer; can operate at 98% of set vs. 90% for spring-loaded No back pressure effect Pilot controls opening — outlet pressure doesn't shift set point Full-open immediately No proportional opening; instantly at full capacity Larger orifice in smaller body No spring constraint on disc size

Applications: - High-pressure gas service where operating pressure is close to set pressure - Large vapor relief requiring minimum simmer - Services with significant back pressure (manifolded relief header)

Limitation: More complex than spring-loaded; pilot can plug in dirty service; requires field testing for pilot valve function verification.

docs.title: 7.5 Rupture Discs
docs.text:
A rupture disc is a non-reclosing pressure relief device — a thin metal disc that bursts at a set pressure and does not reseat. Once ruptured, the system must be shut down to replace it.

When rupture discs are used:

  • In combination with a PRV: The rupture disc is installed upstream of the PRV to protect the PRV seat from corrosive fluid. The disc is sized slightly below the PRV set pressure; if the PRV fails to reseat and leaks, the disc ruptures before the PRV set is reached
  • As the sole relief device: For toxic or hazardous fluids where any PRV simmer is unacceptable; when process fluid would solidify in a PRV; for very low-set-pressure applications where a spring-loaded PRV cannot be built
  • Full-flow discharge: Rupture disc provides zero restriction when open — maximum discharge coefficient

Applied Control's valve shop certifies and repairs PRVs, but rupture discs are replace-on-fail items. The value-add is ensuring the correct disc spec (burst pressure, material, size) is maintained and documented.

docs.title: 7.6 PRV Maintenance and Certification
docs.text: ASME requires that PRVs be tested and certified. A PRV that has not been tested within the required interval cannot be considered reliable and may not satisfy OSHA PSM or process safety documentation requirements.

docs.title: The PRV Life Cycle
docs.text:
1. As-found testing: PRV is removed from service and popped on a test bench at the Applied Control valve shop. As-found set pressure is recorded.
  2. Disassembly and inspection: Disc, nozzle, and spring are inspected. Corrosion, erosion, and seat damage are documented.
  3. Reconditioning: Seats are lapped; springs are replaced if fatigued or corroded; O-rings and soft goods are replaced.
  4. As-left testing: PRV is popped again at the certified set pressure. Test report is generated.
  5. Nameplate and certification: New nameplate is stamped with set pressure and test date by a National Board-certified repair facility.
  6. Return to service: Test report and new tag are provided to the plant for PSM documentation.

Applied Control's National Board Certified valve shop provides full PRV testing, repair, and certification. This is a significant differentiator — most distributors ship PRVs to a factory; Applied Control turns them in days, not weeks, which is critical for turnaround planning.

docs.title: Common PRV Failures
docs.text: Failure mode Cause Remedy Fails to open at set pressure Corroded or stuck disc; spring fatigue Recondition; replace spring Fails to reseat (leaks continuously) Wire-drawn seat; debris on seat Lap seats; clean disc Chattering PRV oversized for service; excessive inlet pressure drop Right-size valve; reduce inlet line pressure drop Set pressure drift Spring relaxation; corrosion; thermal cycling Retest and certify on schedule Frozen open (blowout) Disc eroded by high-velocity discharge; seat debris Replace disc; inspect for upstream contamination

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Pressure relief valves are the last line of defense against overpressure in any process system. Spring-loaded PRVs and PSVs are the most common — set by spring compression, they open at the set pressure and reseat on blowdown. Pilot-operated relief valves provide tighter operating margins and are immune to back pressure effects. Rupture discs provide non-reclosing relief for toxic or corrosive services. API 520 governs sizing; ASME Section VIII governs construction; OSHA PSM requires documentation. docs.title: Chapter 8: Steam Systems & Traps
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Identify the three phases of steam (saturated, superheated, wet) and state the relationship between steam pressure and saturation temperature
  • Understand: Explain why condensate must be removed from steam systems and what happens when condensate accumulates in steam piping
  • Apply: Select the correct steam trap type for a given steam system application (drip leg, tracer, heat exchanger, turbine drain)
  • Analyze: Diagnose a failed-open vs. failed-closed steam trap from temperature and condensate return measurements
  • Evaluate: Justify a steam trap survey and repair program using energy cost savings calculations

docs.title: 8.1 Steam System Fundamentals
docs.text: Steam is one of the most common process utilities — used for heating, tracing, stripping, turbine drive, and direct injection. Understanding steam physics is essential for correct valve selection, sizing, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Steam Phases
docs.text: Phase Description Key characteristics Saturated steam Steam in equilibrium with liquid water at the same pressure Temperature and pressure are linked by steam tables; contains no superheat Superheated steam Steam heated above saturation temperature at the same pressure Temperature > saturation temperature; used for turbines and process heating Wet steam Mixture of saturated steam and water droplets Quality < 1.0; droplets cause erosion; must be dried before turbine admission

docs.title: Pressure-Temperature Relationship
docs.text:
Saturated steam temperature is determined entirely by pressure — from the steam tables:

Pressure (PSIG) Saturation temperature (°F) Latent heat (BTU/lb) 15 250 945 50 298 912 100 338 889 150 366 857 250 406 820 600 490 731

Higher pressure steam carries more energy per pound but at higher temperature. Process heating typically uses 15–150 PSIG; turbine steam is often 600–1500 PSIG superheated.

docs.title: Condensate Formation
docs.text:
As steam gives up its latent heat to the process, it condenses to liquid water (condensate). This condensate must be removed continuously because:

  1. Water hammer: High-velocity steam sweeping condensate creates destructive pressure surges — "water hammer" — that break pipe joints, fittings, and valve bodies
  2. Loss of heat transfer area: Condensate pooling in heat exchangers reduces effective steam surface area
  3. Corrosion: Oxygen in condensate causes pitting corrosion; dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid
  4. Turbine blade erosion: Wet steam or condensate entering a steam turbine erodes blades catastrophically

docs.title: 8.2 Steam Traps
docs.text: A steam trap is an automatic valve that removes condensate and non-condensable gases from steam systems while preventing live steam from passing through. The trap must distinguish between condensate (which it passes) and steam (which it blocks).

docs.title: The Three Steam Trap Operating Principles
docs.text:
1. Mechanical traps — use the density difference between steam and condensate:

  • Float and thermostatic (F&T): A float rises with condensate level, opening a discharge valve. A thermostatic element handles air and CO₂. Best for large condensate loads and heat exchangers.
  • Inverted bucket: A bucket inverted in the trap body — steam keeps the bucket floating (trap closed); condensate fills the bucket, sinking it (trap opens to discharge). Best for high-pressure steam with light condensate loads.

2. Thermodynamic traps — use the difference in thermodynamic properties between steam and condensate:

  • Disc trap (thermodynamic): A disc lifts under condensate (low velocity) and closes under steam (high velocity creates low pressure under disc, holding it shut). Simple, compact, and rugged. Best for tracer lines and drip legs. Susceptible to failure in cold/freezing conditions.

3. Thermostatic traps — use the temperature difference between steam and subcooled condensate:

  • Bimetallic: A bimetallic element expands with temperature, closing the discharge port when near steam temperature; opens when condensate cools. Best for tracing, jacketed pipes, and low-pressure heating.
  • Balanced pressure: A capsule filled with a fluid that vaporizes at steam temperature. Capsule expands to close the trap on steam; condenses below steam temperature, opening the trap. Very sensitive to condensate subcooling.

docs.title: Steam Trap Selection Guide
docs.text: Application Preferred trap type Why Drip legs (main steam lines) Inverted bucket or disc Handles start-up loads; rugged; compact Tracer lines Disc or bimetallic Small condensate load; freeze-resistant bimetallic preferred in cold climates Heat exchangers (modulating) Float and thermostatic Handles variable condensate load; continuous discharge Turbine drains Inverted bucket or float Critical service; must pass condensate without any steam loss Jacketed pipes/reactors Balanced pressure or bimetallic Uniform heating; subcooling prevents steam waste

docs.title: 8.3 Steam Trap Failure Modes
docs.text: Steam traps fail in two directions — each has different consequences and detection methods:

docs.title: Failed Open (Steam Blowing Through)
docs.text:
A failed-open trap passes live steam into the condensate return system, wasting energy.

Symptoms: - Condensate return temperature unusually high downstream of trap - Hissing sound at trap; visual steam plume at discharge (if vented to atmosphere) - Condensate return system overpressured - Higher-than-expected steam consumption with no process change

Detection: - Ultrasonic testing: A failed-open trap produces high-frequency noise from steam flow vs. intermittent condensate discharge sounds - Infrared thermometry: Downstream temperature nearly equal to upstream = steam blowing through - Visual inspection: Steam (not water) at discharge point

Energy cost of a failed-open trap:

A ½" disc trap failing open at 150 PSIG loses approximately 50 lb/hr of steam. At $8/1000 lb steam, that is $3,500/year of wasted energy from a single trap. A plant with 500 traps and 10% failure rate loses $175,000/year.

docs.title: Failed Closed (Condensate Backing Up)
docs.text:
A failed-closed trap blocks condensate drainage — condensate backs up into the steam system.

Symptoms: - Heat exchanger losing capacity (condensate flooding tubes) - Water hammer in steam lines (condensate slug hitting valves and fittings) - Process temperature cannot reach setpoint - Downstream steam temperature lower than expected

Detection: - Upstream temperature high (steam pressure normal); downstream cold = blocked trap - No discharge activity at trap outlet - Ultrasonic: silence at a trap that should be discharging

docs.title: 8.4 Steam Control Valves
docs.text: Steam service is one of the most demanding for control valves because of high temperatures, high pressures, high differential pressures, and the phase-change behavior of steam.

docs.title: Key Steam Valve Selection Criteria
docs.text:
Temperature: Steam at 600 PSIG is saturated at 490°F; superheated steam for turbine service may reach 900–1050°F. Valve body, bonnet, and packing materials must be rated for service temperature:

Temperature range Body material Packing Up to 450°F WCB carbon steel PTFE rings 450–750°F WC6 chrome-moly Graphite rings 750–1050°F WC9 chrome-moly Graphite + high-temp rings

Pressure drop and noise: High-pressure-drop steam produces intense aerodynamic noise. The Fisher WhisperFlo and Whisper III trim designs use staged pressure reduction to keep velocities subsonic, limiting noise below 85 dB(A) at pipe wall.

Condensing steam and water hammer: A steam control valve that closes during periods of condensate accumulation can experience water hammer when it reopens — a slug of liquid is accelerated by the incoming steam. The Fisher EHD (extra heavy duty) steam conditioning valve is designed for direct injection of steam into process streams, handling the condensation shock loads and desuperheating requirements simultaneously.

docs.title: Fisher 657 Actuator on Steam Valves
docs.text: Steam control valves typically use the Fisher 657 (spring-to-open, fail-open) or 667 (spring-to-close, fail-closed) pneumatic actuator. For steam to reboilers and heating services, fail-closed (667) is standard — loss of instrument air stops steam flow rather than flooding the heat exchanger. For steam turbine bypass, fail-open may be required to maintain steam flow to the condenser.

docs.title: 8.5 Fisher 627 Regulator — Self-Contained Pressure Control
docs.text:
For steam distribution headers and utility steam that does not require DCS control, the Fisher 627 pressure-reducing regulator provides self-contained pressure control without a controller, positioner, or instrument air supply:

  • Operation: Downstream pressure acts through a sensing line on a diaphragm that actuates the valve plug directly. The spring sets the target downstream pressure.
  • Accuracy: ±3–5% of set point (adequate for utility steam distribution)
  • No external power required: Fully self-contained; works during power and instrument air failures
  • Range: Set points from 2 PSIG to 400 PSIG; inlet pressure up to 600 PSIG

When to use the 627: - Utility steam let-down stations feeding non-critical heating loads - Remote locations without instrument air - Building heating systems, tank heating, winterization - Backup pressure control where DCS failure should not interrupt steam

When NOT to use the 627: - Tight pressure regulation required (±1% or better) - DCS feedback and logging required - Variable demand requiring responsive control (use DVC6200-equipped control valve)

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Steam systems require understanding of phase behavior — the saturation temperature at any pressure is fixed by thermodynamics, and condensate formation is inevitable. Steam traps automatically remove condensate while blocking live steam. The three trap operating principles (mechanical, thermodynamic, thermostatic) each suit different applications: float-and-thermostatic for heat exchangers, disc traps for drip legs, bimetallic for tracers. Failed-open traps waste energy; failed-closed traps cause water hammer and loss of heat transfer. Steam control valves face extreme temperature and pressure conditions requiring appropriate body materials, graphite packing, and noise-attenuating trim. The Fisher 627 regulator provides self-contained pressure reduction for non-critical utility steam without any external power or air supply.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Actuators and Positioners — Moving the Valve
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Name the three main actuator types and state which is most common in process control
  • Understand: Explain how a spring-diaphragm actuator produces force and why fail-safe action matters
  • Apply: Select the correct actuator size for a given valve thrust requirement
  • Analyze: Interpret a FIELDVUE DVC6200 valve signature and identify what it reveals about valve health
  • Evaluate: Justify the premium cost of a DVC6200 vs. a conventional positioner using diagnostic and loop performance benefits

docs.title: 9.1 The Actuator's Job
docs.text:
The actuator is the muscle of the control valve assembly. It converts the controller's output signal (typically 4–20 mA or pneumatic 3–15 PSIG) into mechanical force and motion — moving the plug, ball, or disk to the position commanded by the controller.

Three requirements an actuator must meet: 1. Sufficient force to stroke the valve against process differential pressure, packing friction, and spring loads 2. Sufficient speed to respond to the process loop's demand 3. Correct fail-safe action — the position the valve moves to on loss of signal or supply

docs.title: 9.2 Pneumatic Actuators — The Industry Standard
docs.text: Pneumatic actuators dominate process control because: - Instrument air is always available in process plants - Spring-diaphragm design is simple, reliable, and self-contained - Inherently fail-safe (spring return on signal loss) - No electrical hazardous area classification required - Force output scales simply with diaphragm area × pressure

docs.title: Fisher 657 Diaphragm Actuator (Spring-to-Open)
docs.text:
The Fisher 657 is the world's most widely deployed pneumatic actuator. It is a spring-to-open, signal-to-close design:

Feature Specification Action Diaphragm case pressurizes → stem moves down (push-down-to-close) Fail action Air fail: spring pushes stem up → valve opens on air failure Spring range 3–15 PSIG, 6–30 PSIG, or custom Sizes 30, 34, 40, 46, 60, 70, 80, 100 in² effective diaphragm area Stroke Up to 4" standard; up to 6" extended Temperature –40°F to +150°F (actuator air space)

Actuator sizing — thrust calculation:

$$F_{required} = F_{packing} + F_{seat} + F_{stem} + F_{unbalance}$$

Where: - F_packing = packing friction (empirical; depends on packing style and stem diameter) - F_seat = seating load required for the specified leakage class (Class V/VI > Class IV) - F_stem = stem area × ΔP (for balanced vs. unbalanced trim) - F_unbalance = differential pressure force across trim if unbalanced design

Fisher's actuator sizing software (ValveLink) performs this calculation and selects the smallest actuator size that meets force requirements with margin.

docs.title: Fisher 667 Diaphragm Actuator (Spring-to-Close)
docs.text:
The Fisher 667 is the spring-to-close, signal-to-open variant:

  • Air pressure pushes stem up → valve opens
  • Air failure → spring pushes stem down → valve closes
  • Correct for fail-closed applications: emergency shutoff, fuel valves, high-pressure gas letdown

Fail-safe selection guide:

Service Preferred fail position Actuator type Fuel or combustion air Fail-closed Fisher 667 (spring-to-close) Coolant/cooling water Fail-open Fisher 657 (spring-to-open) Level control (overflow risk) Fail-closed Fisher 667 Steam to reboiler Fail-closed Fisher 667 Safety system isolation Depends on SIL analysis Per SIL calculation

docs.title: 9.3 Electric Actuators
docs.text:
Electric actuators use an electric motor driving through a gearbox to position the valve. They are preferred when: - No instrument air is available (remote sites, offshore platforms, buildings) - Very precise position control is needed (pharmaceutical batch processes) - High thrust is required without a large pneumatic supply (large gate/globe valves)

Fisher EIM electric actuators cover torques up to 150,000 in-lb for large quarter-turn valves. Features include: - Integral position feedback (potentiometer or encoder) - Limit switches for open/closed position - Handwheel for manual operation during maintenance - HART or FOUNDATION Fieldbus communication options

Trade-offs vs. pneumatic: - Slower stroke speed (seconds to minutes vs. sub-second for pneumatic) - More complex maintenance (motor, gearbox, controls) - Higher purchase cost for comparable thrust - Excellent for slow processes (temperature, large vessel level)

docs.title: 9.4 Hydraulic Actuators
docs.text:
Hydraulic actuators use pressurized oil (typically 1,500–3,000 PSIG) to produce very high force in a compact package. Used for: - Extremely large valves (choke valves, large gate valves, pipeline mainline isolation) - High-cycle rate applications (compressor anti-surge) - Remote deep-sea or high-temperature installations

Fisher YD series hydraulic actuators provide stroke forces up to 100,000 lbf for large subsea valves. Not common in general process plant service.

docs.title: 9.5 Positioners — Closing the Position Loop
docs.text:
A positioner is a local feedback controller that compares the commanded position (from the DCS, 4–20 mA) with the actual position (from the stem position feedback) and modulates the actuating pressure to eliminate any position error.

Without a positioner: The 4–20 mA signal directly loads a current-to-pneumatic (I/P) converter, which sets actuator pressure. Packing friction, supply pressure variations, and stem force changes cause position errors.

With a positioner: The positioner continuously corrects for all of these — it knows where the valve actually is and drives the actuator until the position matches the command.

docs.title: Why Positioners Are Now Standard
docs.text:
On legacy systems, positioners were sometimes omitted to save cost. Today they are standard because:

  1. Tighter control: Position error < 0.5% of span vs. 5–10% without positioner
  2. Diagnostics: Modern positioners (DVC6200) report position, friction, signature, and alert on deviation — impossible without feedback
  3. Split-range control: Two valves controlled on different parts of the 4–20 mA signal requires positioners
  4. HART communication: Enables remote access to valve health data from the DCS workstation

docs.title: 9.6 Fisher FIELDVUE DVC6200 — The Digital Valve Controller
docs.text: The DVC6200 is the flagship positioner from Fisher — the most sophisticated, most widely deployed intelligent positioner in the industry.

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text: Attribute Specification Input signal 4–20 mA HART (standard) or 4–20 mA with HART Feedback Hall-effect travel sensor (contactless, non-wearing) Supply pressure 1.4–10.0 bar (20–145 PSIG) Temperature –40°C to +85°C (–40°F to +185°F) Hazardous area ATEX II 2G, FM Explosionproof, CSA Communication HART Revision 5/7; optional FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS Diagnostics Full valve signature, friction trend, travel deviation, alert history Mounting Direct-mount to Fisher actuators; universal for third-party

docs.title: DVC6200 Diagnostic Capabilities
docs.text:
This is what separates the DVC6200 from any conventional positioner:

1. Valve Signature (Stroke Test) The DVC6200 can perform an automated stroke test while the valve is in service (for non-critical loops) or offline. It records: - Supply pressure - Actuator pressure - Valve travel ...at every point through the full stroke. The resulting signature reveals:

  • Packing friction: Width of the hysteresis loop in the signature
  • Seat condition: Abnormal force signature near seating
  • Actuator spring rate: Slope of the signature — detects spring failure
  • Diaphragm leakage: Pressure hold test identifies air leaks

2. Travel Deviation Alert If the actual valve position deviates from commanded position by more than a set threshold, the DVC6200 raises a Hart alert visible in the DCS or AMS Device Manager. This catches: - Packing sticking - Plug-seat contact preventing full close - Actuator pressure loss

3. Friction Trending The DVC6200 tracks friction over time. A rising friction trend indicates packing wear before it causes control problems. Schedule the maintenance before the failure — not after.

4. Partial Stroke Testing (PST) for SIS For safety-instrumented system valves, the DVC6200 can perform a partial stroke test — moving the valve 10–15% from the fully open position to prove mechanical integrity without disrupting process flow. Required by IEC 61511 for SIL 2 and SIL 3 applications to achieve proof test coverage targets.

Accessing DVC6200 diagnostics

DVC6200 diagnostics are accessed through: - HART handheld (375/475 Field Communicator): For field technicians during commissioning - Emerson AMS Device Manager: Plant-wide asset management; historical trending; alert management - Emerson DeltaV with DVC6200 integration: Real-time HART reads into the DCS historian; alerts appear on operator displays - ValveLink software: Dedicated valve management application; generates PDF reports for compliance documentation

docs.title: 9.7 DVC2000 — Entry-Level Smart Positioner
docs.text:
For less critical service or tighter budgets, the Fisher DVC2000 provides HART communication and basic diagnostics at lower cost:

  • Integral to actuator mounting (direct mount only)
  • HART communication for remote position readout
  • Basic friction and travel deviation alerts
  • No full valve signature capability
  • Appropriate for general process service where signature analysis is not required

docs.title: 9.8 Volume Boosters and Accessories
docs.text:
For fast-stroking applications (anti-surge, emergency shutdown), the positioner's output may not drive actuator pressure fast enough. Volume boosters solve this:

  • A volume booster amplifies the positioner's pilot signal with a high-flow relay
  • The actuator fills and exhausts at high flow rates (fast stroke)
  • The positioner controls precisely, the booster provides the flow capacity
  • Fisher 627 Series volume boosters: flow capacity up to 300 SCFM at 100 PSIG

Accessory ecosystem:

Accessory Function Volume booster Fast stroke speed Trip valve Pneumatic on/off override (ESD) Solenoid valve Electrical on/off isolation of air supply Supply regulator Filters and regulates instrument air to clean, constant pressure Lock-up valve Locks valve position on air supply failure (preserves last position) Limit switches Position feedback to DCS as discrete signal Position transmitter 4–20 mA position feedback to DCS

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Actuators are the muscle of the control valve assembly. Fisher 657 (spring-to-open) and 667 (spring-to-close) diaphragm actuators cover the vast majority of process control applications; fail-safe action is a critical selection criterion. Positioners close the position feedback loop, eliminating errors from packing friction and supply pressure variation. The Fisher DVC6200 FIELDVUE positioner is the industry benchmark — not just for position control precision, but for its diagnostic capabilities: valve signature, friction trending, travel deviation alerts, and partial stroke testing. These diagnostics reduce unplanned downtime, justify maintenance scheduling, and enable SIS proof testing. The DVC6200 is Applied Control's strongest single product for proving value to a plant's maintenance and reliability organization.

Question 2 — Understand

Question 3 — Evaluate

docs.title: Chapter 10: Positioners, Fieldbus & Digital Communication
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Name the three digital communication protocols used with Fisher FIELDVUE devices and state the signal standard for each
  • Understand: Explain how FOUNDATION Fieldbus differs from HART in its control architecture and why this matters for control loop response
  • Apply: Configure a DVC6200 for split-range control on a heating/cooling application using HART ranging commands
  • Analyze: Interpret a DVC6200 valve signature report and identify the key indicators of packing wear, spring degradation, and seat condition
  • Evaluate: Justify the choice between HART, FOUNDATION Fieldbus, and WirelessHART for three different instrumentation scenarios

docs.title: 10.1 The Positioner Revisited
docs.text:
Chapter 9 introduced the positioner as a position feedback controller. This chapter goes deeper into the digital communication layer that transforms positioners from dumb I/P converters into intelligent, diagnostic field devices integrated into the plant's asset management ecosystem.

The shift from pneumatic-only positioners to digital valve controllers (DVCs) is arguably the most important change in control valve technology in the past 30 years. The DVC6200 is not just a more accurate positioner — it is a measurement instrument that reports valve health data continuously to the control room.

docs.title: 10.2 HART Communication — Deep Dive
docs.text: HART (Highway Addressable Remote Transducer) was introduced in Chapter 3 for transmitters. For the DVC6200, HART enables a dramatically richer interaction:

docs.title: HART Variables for DVC6200
docs.text:
Variable HART address Engineering units Diagnostic use Primary Variable (PV) PV % travel Actual valve position Secondary Variable (SV) SV mA Input current (commanded position) Tertiary Variable (TV) TV PSIG Actuator pressure Quaternary Variable (QV) QV PSIG Supply pressure

The DCS can read all four variables simultaneously via HART multi-variable polling — providing a complete picture of valve state from the control room without a field visit.

docs.title: HART-Based DVC6200 Configuration
docs.text:
All DVC6200 configuration is performed over HART — no DIP switches, no potentiometers. Key configurable parameters:

Parameter Function Typical setting Travel range Sets 4 mA position and 20 mA position 0% and 100% travel Action Direct (4mA=closed, 20mA=open) or Reverse Depends on fail-safe design Gain (proportional) Position loop gain — affects response speed 2–4 typical; tune for stability Travel cutoff (low) Tight shutoff below this % — drives to hard seat 1–3% Friction compensation Adds impulse to overcome static friction Enable for high-packing friction Alert thresholds Travel deviation, friction limit, supply pressure low Set per application criticality

docs.title: Split-Range Configuration
docs.text:
In heating/cooling control, a single controller output (4–20 mA) drives two valves — one for heating (steam), one for cooling (coolant). The positioners are ranged to respond to different portions of the signal:

  • Cooling valve: Ranged 4–12 mA (0–100% open) — fully open at 4 mA, closed at 12 mA
  • Heating valve: Ranged 12–20 mA (0–100% open) — closed at 12 mA, fully open at 20 mA

At 12 mA, both valves are closed — the dead band. The DVC6200 split ranging is configured entirely in HART with no hardware modification.

docs.title: 10.3 FOUNDATION Fieldbus
docs.text: FOUNDATION Fieldbus (FF) is a fully digital, two-wire bus protocol that replaces the 4–20 mA analog signal with an all-digital signal. Multiple devices share the same pair of wires; control can execute in the field device itself.

docs.title: How FF Differs from HART
docs.text: Characteristic HART FOUNDATION Fieldbus Signal 4–20 mA + digital overlay All-digital (31.25 kbps, H1) Devices per wire pair 1 (multidrop: up to 15, no analog) 2–32 devices Control execution DCS executes control Can execute in field device (function blocks) Update rate 250–500 ms (digital) 50 ms or faster Interoperability Device-type specific Standardized function blocks (AI, AO, PID)

docs.title: FF Architecture
docs.text:
An FF segment consists of: - H1 segment wire pair at 31.25 kbps - Fieldbus power conditioner — provides segment power and isolates DCS - Up to 32 devices (practical limit: 8–16 for control loops with good response) - Link Active Scheduler (LAS) — manages segment timing; embedded in DCS interface card or in one smart field device

The DVC6200 with FF option contains a PID function block — the entire control loop (measurement input, PID calculation, valve output) can execute within the field device at scan rates as fast as 50 ms, independent of DCS scan rate.

docs.title: When to Choose FF
docs.text:
• New greenfield plant design where a full FF infrastructure is planned from the start
  • Applications requiring sub-100 ms control response independent of DCS scan rate
  • Projects where wire reduction economics are significant (1 wire pair vs. 12+ for 12 devices)
  • Emerson DeltaV-based DCS (DeltaV has the best FF integration of any DCS platform)

docs.title: When HART is Preferred
docs.text:
• Brownfield retrofit (existing 4–20 mA infrastructure)
  • Plants with legacy DCS not supporting FF
  • Applications where the DCS executes all control and FF's field-execution capability is not needed
  • When device variety and procurement flexibility matter (larger HART device ecosystem)

docs.title: 10.4 PROFIBUS PA
docs.text:
PROFIBUS PA (Process Automation) is the IEC 61158 process fieldbus widely used in Europe and in plants with Siemens or ABB DCS systems. Signal standard: 31.25 kbps, two-wire bus, similar to FF H1 physically but with a different protocol layer.

The DVC6200 is available with PROFIBUS PA option for plants operating Siemens PCS7 or ABB 800xA — ensuring Applied Control can serve customers regardless of their DCS platform.

docs.title: 10.5 WirelessHART for Valves
docs.text:
WirelessHART (Chapter 3) can be applied to positioners in monitoring-only scenarios. A wireless adapter (Emerson Wireless THUM) attached to the DVC6200 HART terminals transmits diagnostic data to a WirelessHART gateway without any wired connection.

Applications: - Monitoring valve diagnostics in remote or hard-to-reach locations without running new HART wiring - Adding valve health visibility to legacy pneumatic-only valves (pair with a position transmitter) - Temporary diagnostic campaigns (mount adapters during a survey, remove after)

Limitation: WirelessHART is monitoring-only — the 4–20 mA wired connection still controls the valve. You cannot operate a safety valve or control loop over WirelessHART.

docs.title: 10.6 ValveLink — Valve Management Software
docs.text: Emerson ValveLink is the PC-based valve management application that provides the most complete interface to DVC6200 diagnostics:

docs.title: ValveLink Capabilities
docs.text:
Feature Function Valve signature Graphical display of supply pressure, actuator pressure, and travel through full stroke Step response Tests valve response time to step changes in input — measures hysteresis and deadband Friction analysis Calculates running and static friction from signature data Performance diagnostics Automated analysis of signature vs. baseline — flags deviations Report generation PDF reports suitable for PSM documentation Device configuration Full DVC6200 parameter read/write over HART Offline configuration Build configuration without connecting to device; download when connected

ValveLink runs on a PC connected to a HART modem (USB or serial). It can also operate through AMS Device Manager or DeltaV Live for plant-wide access without dedicated PC cabling.

docs.title: Interpreting a Valve Signature
docs.text:
The valve signature is the graphical fingerprint of a control valve assembly's mechanical health:

Supply pressure (PSIG)
        │
   ─────┼─────────────────────  (flat line = regulator OK)
        │
Actuator│    /─────────────────  (opening stroke)
pressure│   /
(PSIG)  │  /  hysteresis band
        │ /─────────────────────  (closing stroke)
        │/
        └────────────────────── Travel (%)
                 0%           100%

Reading the signature: - Hysteresis band width → packing friction (wider = more friction = wear) - Slope of pressure vs. travel → spring rate (changed slope = spring degradation) - Pressure spike near 0% travel → seat load (excessive spike = over-seating force from oversized actuator) - Irregular steps or jumps → sticky packing or worn stem - Step change in pressure without travel change → diaphragm leak (pressure doesn't hold)

docs.title: 10.7 AMS Device Manager Integration
docs.text:
Emerson AMS Device Manager is the enterprise-level asset management platform that aggregates diagnostic data from all HART and FF field devices across the plant:

Function Description Device health dashboard Color-coded status (OK / Advisory / Maintenance / Failed) for all devices Alert management Routes device alerts to maintenance work orders Historical trending Friction, travel deviation, supply pressure — trended over months/years Scheduled diagnostics Automatically runs valve signature tests on a schedule Calibration management Tracks calibration intervals; generates calibration records Device configuration history Records all configuration changes with timestamp and user

The AMS-DVC6200 combination is Applied Control's most powerful reliability tool. A plant with 200 DVC6200-equipped valves in AMS has continuous health monitoring of every critical valve, with alerts surfacing in the control room before failures occur.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: The DVC6200 FIELDVUE digital valve controller communicates over HART, FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS PA, or WirelessHART — each protocol suited to different plant architectures. HART is the dominant protocol for brownfield and mixed-fleet plants; FF enables field-level control execution and is optimal for greenfield DeltaV plants. The DVC6200's diagnostic value is realized through ValveLink and AMS Device Manager — both providing valve signature analysis, friction trending, and alert management that prevent failures. Valve signatures are the diagnostic fingerprint of every valve's mechanical health: packing friction shows in hysteresis band width, spring condition shows in slope, and seat condition shows in the force profile near closure. This diagnostic ecosystem is the foundation of Applied Control's predictive maintenance value proposition.

docs.text:

docs.title: Chapter 11: Emerson DeltaV DCS & Safety Systems
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Identify the three tiers of the DeltaV system architecture and state the function of each
  • Understand: Explain how DeltaV CHARMs differ from traditional I/O cards and why this reduces installed cost
  • Apply: Describe the engineering workflow for adding a new PID control loop in DeltaV, from I/O assignment through parameter configuration to commissioning

docs.title: 11.1 DeltaV System Architecture Overview
docs.text: Emerson DeltaV is a modern distributed control system (DCS) built on an Ethernet-based architecture with three primary tiers:

docs.title: Tier 1: Field I/O Layer
docs.text:
Physical connection between field devices (transmitters, control valves, on/off valves, motors) and the DeltaV controllers. I/O can be:

  • Traditional I/O cards: Wired to terminal blocks in marshalling cabinets; each card handles 8–16 channels of a specific signal type (AI, AO, DI, DO)
  • CHARM I/O (Electronic Marshalling): Each field wire terminates on a CHARM (Characterization Module) — a per-channel intelligent I/O module that can be any signal type (AI 4–20mA HART, AO, DI, DO) configured in software. No marshalling cabinet; no rewiring to change signal type.

docs.title: Tier 2: Controller Layer
docs.text:
DeltaV Controllers (MD, MD Plus, MX, and S-series) execute the process control strategy:

  • Deterministic scan rate (typically 100–500 ms for process control)
  • Built-in redundancy (primary + secondary controller pairs with bumpless switchover)
  • Direct HART integration — reads secondary variables from HART devices without additional hardware
  • FOUNDATION Fieldbus interface — runs FF segments directly from the controller
  • OPC connectivity to plant historian, MES, and ERP systems

DeltaV Controller sizing:

Controller model I/O capacity Control loops Applications MD 750 I/O ~200 loops Small units, remote skids MD Plus 1200 I/O ~400 loops Medium process units MX 2500 I/O ~800 loops Large process units S-series Scalable 1000+ loops Large integrated systems

docs.title: Tier 3: Workstation / Network Layer
docs.text:
• DeltaV Operate (HMI): Operator interface — process graphics, alarms, trends
  • DeltaV Operate for Batch: Recipe execution, batch reporting
  • DeltaV Insight: Continuous historian; feeds Emerson Asset Management Suite
  • DeltaV Live: Modern HTML5 operator interface replacing legacy DeltaV Operate
  • Engineering workstation: DeltaV Explorer for configuration, DeltaV Diagnostics

docs.title: 11.2 CHARMs Electronic Marshalling — The Game Changer
docs.text:
Traditional DCS I/O requires: 1. Field wire → marshalling cabinet terminal block 2. Jumper wire → specific-type I/O card (AI, AO, DI, DO) 3. I/O card → controller

If a signal type changes (e.g., a 4–20 mA transmitter becomes a HART transmitter, or a digital output needs to change rack location), hardware rewiring is required.

DeltaV CHARMs eliminate marshalling: - Each field wire connects directly to a CHARM I/O module - CHARM type is configured in software — one module handles AI, AO, DI, or DO - CHARMs slide into CIOC (CHARM I/O Card) carriers; carriers connect to controllers via Ethernet - No marshalling cabinet required → significant cost reduction in new construction

CHARM economic impact on a 1,000-point system:

Item Traditional I/O CHARM Marshalling cabinet 4 cabinets × $15,000 Eliminated Rewiring cost (engineering changes) $500/point × 50 changes $0 (software) Installation labor Higher (terminal block jumpers) Lower (one termination) Engineering time Higher (I/O assignment fixed early) Lower (late binding)

Late binding is the key concept: with CHARMs, the I/O type can be determined after field installation, allowing the DCS configuration to proceed in parallel with construction.

docs.title: Function Blocks
docs.text:
DeltaV uses IEC 61499-inspired function blocks for control strategy configuration:

Block Function Common use AI (Analog Input) Reads a process measurement from a field device Any transmitter AO (Analog Output) Writes a control signal to a final element Control valves, VFDs DI / DO Digital input / output Pumps, motors, solenoids PID PID control algorithm All feedback loops Ratio Calculates a ratio between two measured variables Flow ratio control Lead/Lag Dynamic compensation Feedforward, cascade SPLITTER Splits one output to two AO blocks Split-range control Sequence Sequential logic for step-by-step operations Startup/shutdown, batch

docs.title: Building a PID Loop in DeltaV
docs.text:
1. Create module: In DeltaV Explorer, create a Control Module assigned to the appropriate controller
  2. Add I/O: Assign the AI block to the CHARM channel connected to the transmitter; assign the AO block to the CHARM channel connected to the DVC6200
  3. Add PID block: Wire AI → PID → AO
  4. Configure PID: Set Kp, Ti, Td; configure engineering units, scale limits, alarm limits
  5. Configure AO: Set action (direct/reverse), ranging, output limits
  6. Download: Transfer module to controller; controller begins execution
  7. Commission: Place in Auto mode; observe process response; tune PID gains
  8. HART reads: Enable HART secondary variable reads on the AO block to capture DVC6200 diagnostic data into the historian

docs.title: Cascade Control
docs.text:
DeltaV cascade loops connect two PID blocks: the primary (outer) controller sets the setpoint of the secondary (inner) controller. The secondary loop must be at least 5× faster than the primary.

Example: Reactor temperature cascade - Primary: Temperature controller → sets cooling water flow setpoint - Secondary: Flow controller → positions the cooling water control valve

Configuration: Set primary PID output to target the secondary PID's Remote Setpoint parameter.

docs.title: Model Predictive Control (DeltaV PredictPro)
docs.text:
For multi-variable processes with interactions between loops, DeltaV PredictPro implements a model predictive controller (MPC) as a DeltaV module. MPC: - Simultaneously controls multiple outputs (MVs — manipulated variables) - Handles constraints (max/min limits) explicitly - Predicts process response using a dynamic model - Particularly valuable in distillation, reaction, and heat integration systems

Applied Control has DeltaV PredictPro commissioning capability — a significant differentiator in the DCS market.

docs.title: Batch Control (DeltaV Batch)
docs.text: DeltaV Batch implements the ISA-88 batch control standard: - Recipe management: Master, control, and batch recipes - Procedure execution: Procedural elements (procedures, unit procedures, operations, phases) - Equipment arbitration: Allocates shared equipment between concurrent batches - Electronic batch records: Automatic documentation of every parameter and event

docs.title: 11.5 DeltaV Safety Instrumented System (SIS)
docs.text: DeltaV SIS is Emerson's integrated safety system, built on the same platform as DeltaV DCS but architecturally separated to meet IEC 61511 requirements.

docs.title: Safety vs. Basic Process Control
docs.text:
IEC 61511 requires independence between the Safety Instrumented System and the Basic Process Control System:

Requirement DeltaV DCS DeltaV SIS Physical I/O separation Shared (CHARM) Dedicated SIS I/O Controller separation Shared controller Dedicated SIS logic solver Failure independence Not required Required — common cause failure analysis SIL certification Not certified TÜV certified SIL 2/3 capable Proof test requirements None Per IEC 61511

DeltaV SIS Logic Solvers are TÜV-certified, redundant (1oo1D, 1oo2, 2oo3 voting architectures) dedicated controllers for SIS applications.

docs.title: Safety Instrumented Functions (SIFs)
docs.text:
A Safety Instrumented Function (SIF) is a combination of sensor(s), logic solver, and final element(s) designed to achieve a required Safety Integrity Level (SIL):

SIL Probability of Failure on Demand (PFD) Risk reduction factor SIL 1 0.1 – 0.01 10 – 100 SIL 2 0.01 – 0.001 100 – 1,000 SIL 3 0.001 – 0.0001 1,000 – 10,000

docs.title: Partial Stroke Testing in DeltaV SIS
docs.text:
For SIS final elements (shutdown valves), Partial Stroke Testing (PST) is required by IEC 61511 to maintain SIL certification between major proof tests. DeltaV SIS integrates with the Fisher DVC6200 to:

  1. Command the SIS valve to stroke 10–15% from its normal open position
  2. Verify the valve moves (position feedback confirms mechanical integrity)
  3. Return to open position
  4. Log the test result with timestamp for PSM documentation

PST can be performed from the DeltaV SIS engineer workstation without taking the SIS offline — satisfying the proof test coverage requirement with minimal process disruption.

Emerson's Smart Commissioning methodology allows DeltaV to be installed and configured while the plant is still running on the legacy system. docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 — Remember

What does a DeltaV CHARM do that a traditional I/O card cannot?

  • A) It handles more channels per card
  • B) It allows any field wire to be configured as any signal type (AI, AO, DI, DO) in software after installation — eliminating the need to rewire when signal types change

Question 2 — Understand

docs.title: Chapter 12: Flow Measurement
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Name five distinct flow measurement technologies and state the physical principle each uses
  • Understand: Explain why a Coriolis meter measures mass flow directly while an orifice plate measures volume flow, and what additional data is needed to convert between the two
  • Apply: Select the appropriate Rosemount or Micro Motion flow meter for three different services: steam utility header, crude oil custody transfer, and municipal water
  • Analyze: Calculate the actual flow through an orifice plate when the measured ΔP is 45 inH₂O and the calibrated range is 0–100 inH₂O at 500 GPM
  • Evaluate: Justify the higher capital cost of a Micro Motion Coriolis meter over an orifice plate for a chemical batch dosing application

docs.title: 12.1 Why Flow Measurement Matters
docs.text:
Flow is the most frequently measured process variable in industrial plants — more flow loops exist than any other control or measurement function. The economic stakes are high:

  • Custody transfer: Revenue depends on accurate measurement of product sold or purchased
  • Mass balance: Safety and environmental compliance require knowing how much of each component enters and exits a process
  • Batch recipe: Product quality depends on precise flow dosing of reactants
  • Energy efficiency: Steam and fuel metering drives utility cost optimization
  • Environmental reporting: Flare gas, stack emissions, and wastewater discharge are regulated

Measurement error of 1% on a pipeline carrying $10 million/year of product = $100,000/year of mismeasured revenue.

docs.title: 12.2 Differential Pressure Flow — Orifice Plates and Beyond
docs.text: The differential pressure (DP) flow method is the oldest and most widespread flow measurement technology. A primary element in the pipeline creates a controlled pressure drop; the DP transmitter measures this pressure difference, and the flow computer calculates flow from the DP-flow relationship.

docs.title: The DP Flow Equation
docs.text:
For an incompressible (liquid) fluid:

$$Q = C_d \cdot A_2 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2(P_1 - P_2)}{\rho(1 - \beta^4)}}$$

Where: - Q = volumetric flow rate (m³/s or GPM) - Cd = discharge coefficient (0.61 for orifice plate) - A₂ = orifice bore area (m²) - β = beta ratio = d/D (orifice diameter / pipe diameter) - ρ = fluid density (kg/m³)

Key consequence: Flow varies as √ΔP. At 25% of maximum ΔP, flow is 50% of maximum. This creates poor turndown accuracy at low flow — the ΔP at 10% flow is only 1% of the DP at full flow, near the noise floor of most transmitters.

docs.title: Orifice Plate Types
docs.text: Type Description Application Concentric Round hole centered in plate Clean liquids, gases, steam Eccentric Hole offset to bottom of pipe Slurries, dirty fluids Segmental Partial chord opening at bottom Heavy slurries, solids Quadrant edge Radius-edged bore Viscous liquids (Reynolds < 10,000)

docs.title: Rosemount 3051SFC — Integrated DP Flow Transmitter
docs.text:
The Rosemount 3051SFC combines differential pressure, static pressure, and temperature measurement in one device:

  • Compensated mass flow: Uses real-time P and T to correct volumetric DP flow to actual mass flow without an external flow computer
  • Eliminates three separate transmitters (DP, pressure, temperature)
  • HART 7: Reports compensated mass flow, volumetric flow, energy flow (for steam), density, and three raw measurements simultaneously

Annubar primary element (Rosemount 485): The Annubar is a multi-point averaging pitot tube — a bar spanning the pipe with ports at multiple radial positions that average the velocity profile across the pipe. It provides: - Lower permanent pressure loss than an orifice plate - Bidirectional measurement - Simpler installation (tap into pipe vs. removing spool) - Best for large pipe diameters (6"–120")

docs.title: 12.3 Vortex Flow Measurement — Rosemount 8800
docs.text: Chapter 3 introduced the Rosemount 8800D vortex flowmeter. This chapter goes deeper into the application engineering.

docs.title: Vortex Meter Limitations
docs.text:
Minimum velocity requirement: Vortex shedding only occurs above a minimum Reynolds number (Re > 10,000). Below this, vortices are irregular and the meter reads unreliably. This creates a low-flow cutoff — below ~20% of maximum flow, many vortex meters do not output a reliable signal.

No solids tolerance: Particles can coat the bluff body sensor and blunt the vortex shedding, causing dropout. Vortex is not suitable for slurries or dirty liquids with solids above ~50 ppm.

Vibration sensitivity: External vibration on the pipe can be misinterpreted as vortex shedding. The 8800D uses a dual-sensor approach that cancels mechanical vibration while retaining the fluid vortex signal — it is significantly more vibration-immune than single-sensor competitors.

docs.title: Vortex for Steam — The Primary Application
docs.text:
Vortex is the preferred technology for steam flow because: - Steam is hot, clean, and single-phase (when properly dried) - No moving parts to corrode or scale - High Reynolds numbers in steam (Re >> 10,000 typical) - Multivariable version provides compensated mass flow for billing and energy calculations

The Rosemount 8800D MVD (Multivariable) integrates: - Vortex sensor (velocity/volumetric flow) - Integral temperature sensor (RTD) - Integral static pressure sensor - Internal flow computer: calculates compensated steam mass flow, energy flow (BTU/hr), and condensate flow — replaces 3 separate transmitters plus an external flow computer

docs.title: 12.4 Coriolis Flow Measurement — Micro Motion
docs.text:
The Coriolis effect is the deflection experienced by a mass moving within a rotating reference frame. In a Coriolis flowmeter, a vibrating tube replaces the rotating reference frame:

  1. A driver causes the flow tube to vibrate at its natural frequency
  2. Fluid flowing through the tube has momentum (mass × velocity)
  3. The flowing mass resists the change in direction caused by vibration
  4. This creates a measurable twist (phase shift) between inlet and outlet sensors
  5. The phase shift is proportional to mass flow rate — directly, with no density correction required

docs.title: Coriolis Performance Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Specification (ELITE series) Mass flow accuracy ±0.05% of rate Density accuracy ±0.0005 g/cc Temperature (process) ±1°C Turndown 100:1 (liquid), 20:1 (gas) Fluids Any liquid, slurry, or dense gas Process connection ¼" to 6" Outputs Mass flow, volume flow, density, temperature, viscosity (select models) Communication HART 7, FOUNDATION Fieldbus, PROFIBUS PA, Modbus

docs.title: Why Coriolis Wins — Application Cases
docs.text:
Custody transfer: The API MPMS standard Chapter 6 recognizes Coriolis as a primary standard for liquid petroleum measurement. ±0.05% accuracy with no density correction and no requirement for flow conditioning (no straight-run requirements) makes it the highest-accuracy, lowest-uncertainty liquid meter available.

Batch dosing: In a batch reactor, each reactant must be added in precise mass quantities regardless of temperature, density, or viscosity changes during filling. Coriolis measures actual mass — when the flow computer totalizer reaches the target, the valve closes. No density or temperature correction needed; no batch variance from composition change.

Density measurement: Real-time density from a Coriolis meter enables concentration calculation for many binary mixtures (ethanol/water, NaOH/water, acid solutions). One meter replaces a flow meter + density meter + concentration calculation system.

docs.title: 12.5 Magnetic Flow Measurement
docs.text:
A magnetic flowmeter (magmeter) measures the velocity of a conductive fluid by measuring the EMF induced when the fluid (acting as a conductor) moves through a magnetic field (Faraday's law):

$$E = B \cdot D \cdot V$$

Where E = induced EMF (mV), B = magnetic field strength, D = pipe diameter, V = fluid velocity.

Key requirement: The fluid must be electrically conductive — minimum ~5 μS/cm. This excludes hydrocarbons and most gases.

Advantages: - No restriction in the flow path → zero permanent pressure loss - Full-bore measurement → tolerates solids, slurries, and fibrous materials - Bidirectional measurement - Unaffected by density, viscosity, or temperature changes

Applications: Water and wastewater, slurry, pulp and paper, chemical (aqueous), pharmaceutical (conductive fluids), mining.

Rosemount 8750W magnetic flowmeter for water/wastewater service: Offers empty-pipe detection (alarm when pipe drains), bidirectional flow, and reduced-bore option for higher velocity.

docs.title: 12.6 Ultrasonic Flow Measurement
docs.text:
Ultrasonic flowmeters measure fluid velocity using the time-of-flight of ultrasonic pulses transmitted diagonally across the pipe: - Downstream pulse arrives faster (added by fluid velocity) - Upstream pulse arrives slower (opposed by fluid velocity) - Difference in transit time = velocity

Clamp-on ultrasonic: Transducers mount externally on the pipe — no pipe penetration, no wetted parts. Ideal for large pipes (6"–60"+), non-invasive measurement on existing piping, and temporary flow verification surveys.

Spoolpiece ultrasonic (custody grade): Transducers are in the pipe wall in precision-machined ports. Multiple path (3–6 chords) averaging corrects for velocity profile distortions. Used for high-accuracy gas custody transfer (pipeline metering stations, custody LNG).

Rosemount 3107: Submersible clamp-on for water and wastewater; rated for buried installations.

docs.title: 12.7 Thermal Mass Flow Measurement
docs.text:
A thermal mass flowmeter measures the heat required to maintain a heated sensor at a constant temperature above the flowing fluid — more mass flow = more heat required = higher power draw.

$$P = c_p \cdot \dot{m} \cdot \Delta T$$

Applications: Low-flow gas measurement (instrument air, nitrogen, hydrogen, natural gas in small lines), flare gas monitoring.

Rosemount 3051SFP Annubar + CDS transmitter as a combined thermal mass flow system for flare gas — measures mass flow of low-pressure mixed-composition flare gas streams for environmental reporting.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Flow measurement encompasses more distinct physical principles than any other process measurement category. DP with an orifice plate is universal but limited by √ΔP turndown. Vortex is the preferred steam flow technology — rugged, no moving parts, multivariable mass flow compensation. Coriolis provides the highest accuracy mass flow measurement, direct density measurement, and 100:1 turndown for custody transfer and batch applications. Magnetic meters cover conductive liquids with zero pressure drop and full solids tolerance. Ultrasonic enables non-invasive measurement on large pipes. The Rosemount and Micro Motion product families cover every flow application from water mains to crude oil custody transfer, all communicating over HART or FOUNDATION Fieldbus to AMS Device Manager and DeltaV.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
Question 1 — Apply

An orifice plate flow meter is calibrated for 0–500 GPM at 0–100 inH₂O DP. The measured DP is 45 inH₂O. What is the actual flow?

  • A) 225 GPM (45% of 500)
  • B) 250 GPM (50% of 500)
  • C) 335 GPM — Q = 500 × √(45/100) = 500 × 0.671 = 335 GPM
  • D) 45 GPM

Question 2 — Understand

A process engineer asks why a Coriolis meter doesn't need a density correction for mass flow while an orifice plate does. What is the explanation?

  • A) A Coriolis meter measures the inertia of the flowing mass directly via the Coriolis effect — the phase shift between sensor signals is proportional to mass flow rate itself, regardless of fluid density or composition. An orifice plate measures velocity (via DP), so converting to mass flow requires multiplying by density, which must be measured or assumed.
  • B) Coriolis meters use a compensating temperature sensor
  • C) Orifice plates only work for gases
  • D) Coriolis meters are always more accurate

Question 3 — Evaluate

A specialty chemical plant doses three liquid reagents into a batch reactor. Each reagent has a different density that varies ±5% based on temperature and concentration during filling. The batch recipe requires ±0.1% mass dosing accuracy. Which meter type is required, and why?

  • A) Coriolis (Micro Motion) — because Coriolis measures mass flow directly, density variations have zero effect on accuracy. A DP or vortex meter measuring volume flow would accumulate mass error proportional to the density variation (±5% density = ±5% mass error), which is 50× the required accuracy.
  • B) Orifice plate with density correction
  • C) Vortex with temperature compensation
  • D) Magnetic meter

docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: State the accuracy specification of the Rosemount 3051 pressure transmitter and identify its three model variants

  • Apply: Select the correct level measurement technology for three different applications: an open water sump, a pressurized reactor with foam, and an interface between oil and water

docs.title: 13.1 Pressure Measurement — Deep Dive
docs.text: Chapter 3 introduced the Rosemount 3051 pressure transmitter family. This chapter provides the application engineering depth needed to specify, install, and troubleshoot pressure measurement in demanding services.

docs.title: Absolute, Gauge, and Differential Pressure
docs.text:
Type Definition Symbol Zero reference Absolute pressure Pressure above perfect vacuum PSIA Perfect vacuum (0 PSIA) Gauge pressure Pressure above local atmospheric PSIG Local atmospheric (~14.7 PSIA) Differential pressure Difference between two pressures PSID Any reference point Vacuum (negative gauge) Pressure below atmospheric in Hg vac, PSIA Atmospheric

Rosemount 3051C measures differential pressure (most versatile — used for DP flow, DP level, and process ΔP). Rosemount 3051T measures gauge or absolute pressure. Rosemount 3051L is flanged for direct tank/vessel mounting for liquid level.

docs.title: Installation Considerations
docs.text:
Impulse line design:

Impulse lines connect the process tap to the transmitter sensing element. Improper impulse line design is the leading cause of pressure measurement error in the field:

Problem Cause Solution Plugged impulse line Process fluid solidifying or scaling in line Remote seal; heated impulse line; purge system Liquid-filled line in gas service Condensate accumulates in low point Slope lines to drain; install drain legs Gas-filled line in liquid service Air bubble trapped in high point Install vent at high point; slope lines to transmitter Freezing Cold ambient temperature Insulate and heat trace impulse lines

Manifold valves: A 3-valve or 5-valve manifold allows: - Isolating the transmitter from process for maintenance - Equalizing high and low sides to check zero - Venting the sensing element for calibration

docs.title: Reference Accuracy vs. Installed Accuracy
docs.text:
The Rosemount 3051 reference accuracy of ±0.065% is measured at: - Constant temperature (23°C ± 2°C) - Constant supply voltage - Mid-range calibration span

In installed conditions, additional error terms apply: - Thermal zero effect: ±0.01% of URL per 10°C from reference - Span effect: ±0.01% of reading per 10°C - Static pressure effect (for DP transmitters): ±0.15% of reading per 1000 PSIG

Total installed accuracy for a typical process application is typically ±0.1–0.2% — still among the best in the industry.

docs.title: RTD Wiring Configurations
docs.text:
RTDs are affected by the resistance of lead wires. Three wiring configurations address this:

2-wire: Lead wire resistance adds directly to RTD resistance measurement. Acceptable only for short leads or when ±1°C accuracy is sufficient.

3-wire: Third wire allows the transmitter to measure and subtract one lead wire resistance. Assumes both leads have equal resistance — accurate to ±0.1°C with equal-gauge wires of same length.

4-wire: Separate current and voltage leads — Kelvin connection completely eliminates lead wire effect. Used for laboratory and highest-accuracy process applications.

The Rosemount 644 transmitter supports 2, 3, and 4-wire RTD connections, configured via HART.

docs.title: Thermowell Selection and Wake Frequency
docs.text:
A thermowell is a pressure-tight well inserted into the process that houses the temperature sensor. It protects the sensor from process pressure, velocity, and chemistry while allowing sensor removal without process shutdown.

Wake frequency (Strouhal resonance): Fluid flowing past the thermowell creates vortices at a frequency proportional to velocity. If this wake frequency equals the thermowell's natural resonant frequency, the thermowell can vibrate destructively — a failure mode that has caused process shutdowns and sensor failures.

ASME PTC 19.3 TW-2016 governs thermowell wake frequency analysis. For high-velocity service (steam, gas flow > 50 ft/s), the thermowell must be analyzed to confirm:

$$f_{wake} \neq f_{natural}$$

Thermowell selection factors: - Process temperature and pressure (determines material and wall thickness) - Process velocity (determines wake frequency analysis requirement) - Process fluid (corrosion — 316SS for most, Hastelloy for acids, ceramic for extreme temp) - Insertion length (must reach past boundary layer into bulk flow) - Connection size (matching process nozzle — typically ¾" or 1" NPT/flanged)

docs.title: DP Level Measurement
docs.text:
The hydrostatic head created by a liquid column in a vessel is measured by a differential pressure transmitter:

$$\Delta P = \rho \cdot g \cdot H$$

Where H = liquid height, ρ = liquid density, g = gravitational constant.

Wet leg vs. dry leg:

  • Dry leg (gas reference): The low-pressure tap connects to vapor space above the liquid. Works for open vessels or closed vessels where the vapor will not condense in the reference leg.
  • Wet leg (liquid reference): The low-pressure tap is filled with a reference liquid (seal fluid or process condensate) maintained at a constant level. Required when process vapor condenses in the reference leg (common in steam/hot liquid vessels).

Density effect on DP level accuracy:

If the process fluid density changes (temperature, concentration, or phase change), the measured DP no longer represents actual level:

$$H_{actual} = H_{measured} \cdot \frac{\rho_{calibrated}}{\rho_{actual}}$$

Example: A tank calibrated for water (SG=1.0) containing a process fluid at SG=0.85 will read 18% high. This is a significant source of error in variable-composition services (reactors, distillation column sumps).

Solution for variable-density service: - Use a Coriolis or nuclear density measurement to compensate DP level readings in real time - Use radar (non-density-dependent) instead of DP for level

docs.title: Float and Displacer Level
docs.text:
A float rides on the liquid surface; its position is transmitted mechanically or magnetically to an external indicator or transmitter. Simple, reliable, but limited to clear liquids without foam, coating, or turbulence.

A displacer is a cylinder heavier than the liquid that hangs from a torque tube. As liquid level rises, buoyancy increases, rotating the torque tube. Fisher Level-Trol™ displacer instruments were industry standards for decades and are still in service in many plants.

Limitation: Displacers calibrate for a specific liquid density. Density change = level reading error. Modern preference is guided wave radar for most displacer replacement applications.

docs.title: Guided Wave Radar (GWR) — Rosemount 5300
docs.text:
Guided Wave Radar transmits a microwave pulse (TDR — Time Domain Reflectometry) down a probe into the vessel. The pulse reflects off the liquid surface (or liquid/liquid interface) due to the dielectric discontinuity:

$$L = \frac{c \cdot t}{2\varepsilon_r^{0.5}}$$

Where c = speed of light, t = time of flight, εᵣ = dielectric constant of vapor space.

GWR advantages: - Immune to pressure, temperature, vapor space composition - Measures liquid/liquid interface (oil/water) — two echoes on one probe - Works with foam (RF pulse penetrates foam better than radar) - Works in bypass chambers, stilling wells, and bridles - Accuracy: ±3mm

GWR probe types:

Probe Application Rigid single rod Short-to-medium vessels, clean liquids Rigid twin parallel Better signal in low-dielectric fluids Coaxial Highest accuracy; works in liquids with εᵣ > 1.4 Flexible cable Tall vessels; coiled at bottom to prevent damage

Rosemount 5301: Basic GWR for general liquids. Rosemount 5302: Interface measurement (oil/water/emulsion layers). Rosemount 5303: High-temperature, high-pressure service (up to 450°C, 400 bar).

docs.title: Non-Contact Radar — Rosemount 5408
docs.text:
The Rosemount 5408 is Emerson's flagship non-contact radar level transmitter:

  • 80 GHz FMCW radar: High frequency = narrow beam angle (3°–5°) → works in vessels with internal obstructions (agitators, heating coils, baffles)
  • FMCW (Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave): Continuously transmits a frequency-swept signal; measures level from the frequency difference between transmitted and reflected signals — highly accurate, insensitive to dust, vapor, and condensation
  • Accuracy: ±1 mm reference accuracy
  • Range: Up to 30 meters
  • Application: All liquid services; solids surface measurement; no product contact

When to choose 5408 over 5300 GWR: - Toxic or corrosive liquids where probe insertion is undesirable (HF acid, chlorine) - Strong agitation that would damage a probe - Vessels where probe installation is mechanically difficult - Solids (granules, powders) level measurement - Where zero maintenance contact is required

docs.title: pH Measurement
docs.text:
pH measures hydrogen ion concentration — a logarithmic scale from 0 (strongly acidic) to 14 (strongly alkaline):

$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[H^+]$$

pH measurement requires: - pH glass electrode: Measures EMF proportional to H⁺ activity - Reference electrode: Provides a stable reference potential - Temperature sensor: Temperature compensation (pH is temperature-dependent) - pH transmitter: Converts millivolt signal to 4–20 mA; provides temperature compensation

Rosemount pH sensor line: Includes in-line, submersion, and retractable designs for varying process conditions (pressure, temperature, abrasion).

Maintenance requirement: pH electrodes have a finite life (6–18 months typical) and require regular calibration (pH 4 and pH 7 buffer solutions). This is a high-maintenance measurement — automated calibration systems reduce labor burden.

docs.title: Conductivity Measurement
docs.text: Conductivity measures the ability of a solution to conduct electrical current — directly proportional to dissolved ion concentration. Used for: - Boiler water purity monitoring - RO/DI water quality verification - Acid/base concentration measurement - Ion exchange resin exhaustion detection

docs.title: Dissolved Oxygen (DO)
docs.text: DO measurement is critical in biological wastewater treatment — DO must be maintained in the correct range for aerobic bacteria activity. Optical DO sensors (luminescence-based) have largely replaced electrochemical Clark cells because they: - Don't consume oxygen during measurement - Require minimal maintenance (no membrane to replace) - Drift very little between calibrations

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Pressure measurement begins with the Rosemount 3051 family — 3051C for differential, 3051T for gauge/absolute, 3051L for flanged level. Installed accuracy depends on proper impulse line design — the leading source of error is poor mechanical installation, not transmitter performance. Temperature measurement requires RTD wiring configuration selection and thermowell wake frequency analysis for high-velocity service. Level measurement technology selection depends on fluid properties (density stability, conductivity, corrosivity, foam, turbulence) — GWR for most process liquids, non-contact radar for toxic/corrosive/agitated services, DP for simple clean-liquid services where density is known. Process analysis — pH, conductivity, dissolved oxygen — extends the measurement layer into quality and environmental compliance monitoring.

Every plant has displacer-type level instruments on distillation columns, fractionators, and reactors that have drifted from their calibrated density and are reading incorrectly. The GWR/radar upgrade conversation writes itself: 'Your level instruments calibrated for SG=0.72 — what is your current sump composition?'
  2. Thermowell failures are a safety and reliability issue. A thermowell failure in high-velocity steam or gas creates an immediate process hazard (sensor falls into the process) and a process shutdown. Applied Control can provide the wake frequency analysis (per ASME PTC 19.3 TW) that identifies at-risk thermowells — this is a genuine safety service, not just product upsell.
  3. pH probe maintenance programs create recurring revenue. Any plant with pH loops has a regular probe replacement and calibration need. Applied Control can supply Rosemount pH probes and offer a calibration service program — quarterly visits, calibration documentation, probe replacement on schedule.

Nuclear gauges require NRC licensing, radiation survey, and strict personnel safety protocols. docs.text:
Learning Objectives

  • Remember: Define the four maintenance strategies (reactive, preventive, predictive, reliability-centered) and state which produces the lowest total cost

  • Apply: Interpret a DVC6200 friction trend showing 300% increase over 12 months and determine the appropriate maintenance action and timing
