docs.title: 14.1 The Reliability Imperative
docs.text:
Unplanned downtime is the most expensive event in a process plant. Industry benchmarks:

Industry Cost per hour of unplanned downtime Oil refinery $50,000–$200,000 Chemical plant $20,000–$100,000 Power generation $30,000–$150,000 Pharmaceutical $100,000–$500,000 Pulp and paper $15,000–$50,000

Control valves are the #1 cause of process-related downtime — more shutdowns trace to valve failures than any other single component type. Yet most plants still practice reactive maintenance — they fix valves after they fail.

docs.title: Reactive Maintenance (Run-to-Failure)
docs.text:
The valve is not serviced until it fails or causes a process problem.

Cost structure: Low routine cost, very high corrective cost. Emergency repair includes: unplanned labor (overtime), expedited parts, lost production, potential safety incident.

When appropriate: For non-critical valves with no production impact and low repair cost (utilities, bypasses, low-cost isolations).

docs.title: Preventive Maintenance (Time-Based)
docs.text:
Valves are serviced on a fixed schedule regardless of actual condition — for example, every 2 years pull and inspect all critical valves.

Problem: Over-maintains healthy valves (wastes labor) while under-maintaining deteriorating valves that fail between PM intervals.

docs.title: Predictive Maintenance (Condition-Based)
docs.text:
Valves are serviced when diagnostic data indicates deterioration has reached an action threshold — before failure occurs but without unnecessary early intervention.

Tool: DVC6200 friction trending. A valve with friction at 110% of baseline is fine; at 200% it's worth watching; at 350% it needs repacking before it begins to oscillate.

Result: Fewer total maintenance interventions; no unexpected failures; right part, right time, planned labor.

docs.title: Reliability-Centered Maintenance (RCM)
docs.text:
A formal methodology that identifies the failure modes of each asset, the consequence of each failure, and the optimal maintenance strategy for each failure mode. RCM selects from: - Condition monitoring (predictive) - Scheduled inspection (preventive) - Run-to-failure (reactive) - Design change (eliminate the failure mode)

RCM produces the optimum maintenance plan but requires significant engineering effort. Most plants apply simplified RCM principles to critical equipment.

docs.title: 14.3 AMS Device Manager — The Reliability Platform
docs.text: Emerson AMS Device Manager aggregates HART and FOUNDATION Fieldbus diagnostic data from all field devices across the plant into a centralized asset management platform. For control valves, AMS provides:

docs.title: Device Health Monitoring
docs.text:
Every DVC6200 in the plant reports its status continuously:

Status Meaning Action required Good / Active Device functioning normally; no alerts None Advisory Minor issue detected; monitor Schedule inspection Maintenance Significant alert; degradation confirmed Plan maintenance within 30–60 days Failed Device reporting fault; potential loss of control Immediate response

The AMS dashboard shows all devices color-coded by status. A maintenance technician looking at 200 valves can see at a glance which ones need attention — without visiting a single device in the field.

docs.title: Historical Trending
docs.text: AMS stores the complete history of every diagnostic parameter for every device. docs.title: 14.4 The Applied Control Valve Health Program
docs.text: Applied Control offers a structured valve health program that converts the DVC6200+AMS diagnostic capability into a managed service:

docs.title: Phase 1: Baseline
docs.text:
Objective: Establish the mechanical baseline for every critical valve.

Activities: - DVC6200 installation (if not present) or verification of existing DVC6200 configuration - Full valve signature for each critical valve (offline preferred; online where possible) - AMS configuration: device tags, alert thresholds, reporting structure - Baseline report: friction level, signature shape, spring condition for each valve

docs.title: Phase 3: Turnaround Support

Objective: Use diagnostic data to plan turnaround work scope accurately.

Activities: - Pre-turnaround review: which valves need repair based on friction trends and alert history - Applied Control valve shop: pull, inspect, recondition, repack, and test all flagged valves - Post-turnaround baselines: new signatures after repair confirm work quality - PRV certification: simultaneous PRV testing during turnaround window

Deliverable: Precise turnaround scope (no over-maintenance, no missed maintenance); post-repair baseline signatures; PRV test certificates.

docs.title: Case 1: Rising Friction Trend
docs.text:
Data: DVC6200 friction trend on a 2" Fisher ED globe valve controlling feedwater flow. Baseline friction 18 PSIG (2018). Current friction 61 PSIG (2023). Trend rate: ~9 PSIG/year.

Interpretation: Packing is wearing — friction has tripled over 5 years. At the current rate, friction will exceed the AMS alert threshold (75 PSIG) in approximately 18 months. The valve is likely in the beginning of increased travel deviation during process upsets.

Recommendation: Schedule packing replacement during the next planned outage (12 months out). Do not wait for failure — at 5× baseline friction, the valve will begin to affect loop performance noticeably.

Applied Control action: Schedule shop repair; order packing kit for the ED body; plan a 4-hour maintenance window.

docs.title: Case 2: Sudden Friction Change
docs.text:
Data: DVC6200 friction alert on a 4" Fisher EZ control valve — friction jumped from 22 PSIG to 145 PSIG overnight. No gradual trend.

Interpretation: A sudden friction change is not packing wear — packing wear is gradual. This pattern indicates: foreign object in valve body; process solid accumulation in seat area; trim damage from cavitation event; packing extrusion (packing has been over-tightened or thermally damaged).

Recommendation: Immediate inspection. Pull valve; inspect body cavity and trim for debris or damage. Do not continue operating with 145 PSIG friction — the valve is likely not responding correctly to control signals.

docs.title: Case 3: Valve Signature Shows Diaphragm Leak
docs.text:
Data: Valve signature on a Fisher 657 actuator/DVC6200 assembly shows: during the pressure hold test portion of the signature, actuator pressure drops 8 PSIG over 60 seconds without any stem movement.

Interpretation: The actuator is leaking air — either through the diaphragm or through the upper housing seal. A 8 PSIG drop in 60 seconds is significant enough to affect control in high-friction applications and will worsen.

Recommendation: Replace actuator diaphragm. This is a 2-hour field repair — Applied Control technician on site with the diaphragm kit.

docs.title: Case 4: Spring Degradation
docs.text:
Data: Valve signature slope analysis: the actuator pressure vs. travel slope has flattened — it takes 12 PSIG to compress the spring at zero travel but the spring rate shows only 0.08 PSIG/% travel vs. 0.18 PSIG/% travel at baseline.

Interpretation: The actuator spring has fatigued or broken. A degraded spring means the fail-safe force is reduced — if instrument air fails, the valve may not fully open or close as designed.

Recommendation: Immediate replacement. For a fail-closed valve (safety application), reduced spring force is a safety finding. For a fail-open cooling valve, reduced spring force may prevent full opening on air failure — loss of cooling.

docs.title: 14.6 Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and Valve Reliability Analysis
docs.text:
MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average time between failures for a repairable asset:

$$\text{MTBF} = \frac{\text{Total operating hours}}{\text{Number of failures}}$$

Fisher control valves in typical process service have MTBFs ranging from: - 5–8 years: Standard service (ambient temperature, clean fluid, moderate cycling) - 3–5 years: Severe service (cavitation, high ΔP, corrosive fluid) - 1–3 years: Very severe service (extreme temperature, abrasive slurry, corrosive with high velocity)

DVC6200 diagnostic impact on MTBF: Plants with active friction monitoring and predictive maintenance programs report 40–60% improvement in MTBF for their critical valve population — not because the valves wear less, but because interventions happen at the right time, preventing failures.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Standards, Codes & Compliance
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

docs.title: 15.1 Why Standards Matter in Valve Automation
docs.text:
Standards and codes govern virtually every aspect of the products Applied Control sells and services. A sales engineer who can reference the relevant standard is demonstrating expertise and credibility — a sales engineer who doesn't know which standard applies is demonstrating the opposite.

Three categories:

Category Definition Examples Codes Mandatory requirements enforced by law or regulation ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPVC), OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 Standards Consensus documents — mandatory only when referenced in a contract or code IEC 61511, API 520, IEC 60534 Guidelines Recommended practices — informational only API 521, ISA-TR96.05

docs.title: ASME B16.34 — Valves — Flanged, Threaded, and Welding End
docs.text:
ASME B16.34 is the governing standard for pressure-temperature ratings of industrial valves. It defines: - Pressure classes: Class 150, 300, 600, 900, 1500, 2500 (ANSI classes for flanged end valves) - Pressure-temperature rating tables for each material group and class - Testing requirements: Shell test, seat test, and backseat test procedures - Materials: Acceptable materials for each service temperature range

Reading a valve's pressure class:

A Fisher ED control valve rated Class 300 in WCC (carbon steel) body has: - Maximum allowable pressure at 100°F: 720 PSIG - Maximum allowable pressure at 400°F: 655 PSIG - Maximum allowable pressure at 750°F: 410 PSIG

The pressure rating decreases with temperature — this relationship is defined in ASME B16.34 material group tables.

docs.title: ANSI/FCI 70-2 — Valve Leakage Classification
docs.text:
ANSI/FCI 70-2 (now incorporated in IEC 60534-4) defines the standard leakage classes:

Class Maximum leakage Test method I No test required — II 0.5% of rated Cv Water at 50–125 PSID III 0.1% of rated Cv Water at 50–125 PSID IV 0.01% of rated Cv Water at 50–125 PSID V 5×10⁻⁴ mL/min × PSID × in seat dia Water at max operating ΔP VI Bubble-tight (table by seat size) Air/N₂ at 50 PSIG or max ΔP

Fisher standard offerings by trim design: - Standard metal seat: Class IV - Cavitrol/WhisperFlo trim: Class IV - Soft seat (PTFE/elastomer): Class VI - Class V: Available on request for specific Fisher models

docs.title: 15.3 IEC 60534 — Industrial-Process Control Valves
docs.text:
IEC 60534 is the international control valve standard. Its parts cover:

Part Subject IEC 60534-1 Terminology and general considerations IEC 60534-2-1 Flow capacity: sizing equations for incompressible and compressible fluids IEC 60534-2-3 Test procedures to verify flow capacity IEC 60534-3-1 Dimensions of face-to-face and end-to-end for flanged valves IEC 60534-4 Leakage classification (equivalent to ANSI/FCI 70-2) IEC 60534-8-3 Aerodynamic noise calculation IEC 60534-8-4 Hydrodynamic noise calculation

The sizing equations in IEC 60534-2-1 are the foundation of all Cv-based valve sizing (Chapters 5 and beyond). Fisher's ValveLink sizing software implements these equations.

docs.title: 15.4 API Standards for Pressure Relief
docs.text:
Standard Scope API 520 Part I Sizing of pressure relieving devices API 520 Part II Installation of pressure relieving devices API 521 Guide for pressure-relieving and depressuring systems API 526 Standard flanged steel pressure relief valves (orifice sizes, dimensions) API 527 Seat tightness of pressure relief valves API 576 Inspection of pressure-relieving devices

API 576 is the most operationally relevant for Applied Control's valve shop: - Defines inspection and testing intervals for PRVs - Requires documentation of as-found and as-left test conditions - Specifies acceptable as-found tolerances (±5% of set pressure for most valves) - Guides repair scope (when to recondition vs. replace)

docs.title: 15.5 IEC 61511 — Functional Safety for SIS
docs.text: IEC 61511 (equivalent to ISA-84 in the US) is the process sector application standard for Safety Instrumented Systems. It defines requirements for the entire safety lifecycle:

docs.title: Safety Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Hazard and risk analysis — identify process hazards (HAZOP, LOPA)
  2. Safety requirements specification — define SIL requirements for each SIF
  3. SIS design — select sensors, logic solver, final elements to achieve the SIL
  4. SIS installation and commissioning — install per design; document as-built
  5. SIS validation — demonstrate SIL achievement through testing
  6. SIS operation and maintenance — proof testing, management of change
  7. SIS modification — change control; re-validation
  8. SIS decommissioning — safe disposal of safety functions

docs.title: Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA)
docs.text:
LOPA is the quantitative risk analysis method most commonly used to determine SIL requirements:

  1. Identify the initiating event (e.g., operator error, control valve failure)
  2. Identify the consequence (explosion, toxic release, equipment damage)
  3. Assess the consequence severity and frequency of the initiating event
  4. Identify existing independent protection layers (IPLs) that reduce risk
  5. Calculate the residual risk after IPLs
  6. If residual risk exceeds tolerable risk → SIS required; SIL determined by required risk reduction

Required SIL example:

Initiating event frequency: 0.1/year. Consequence: catastrophic (requires 10⁻⁶/year tolerable risk). Existing IPLs reduce by 10⁻³. Residual risk without SIS: 10⁻⁴/year. Target: 10⁻⁶/year. Required risk reduction by SIS: 100 → SIL 2 (10⁻² to 10⁻³ PFD range).

docs.title: Proof Testing Requirements
docs.text:
Proof test = a functional test that confirms the SIS will respond correctly to a demand. IEC 61511 requires proof testing at an interval determined by the SIL target:

SIL Required test interval (typical) Test coverage SIL 1 Every 1–5 years >60% dangerous failures detected SIL 2 Every 1–3 years >90% dangerous failures detected SIL 3 Every 6 months–1 year >99% dangerous failures detected

PST contribution to proof test coverage: Partial stroke testing of SIS valves detects mechanical failures in the valve assembly (stuck stem, failed actuator). A PST with DVC6200 provides approximately 50–60% proof test coverage for the final element, reducing the frequency of full proof tests (complete valve stroke to closed, which may require process shutdown).

docs.title: 15.6 OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM)
docs.text: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM) is US federal law applicable to facilities that use highly hazardous chemicals above threshold quantities. PSM has 14 elements; several directly involve Applied Control:

docs.title: Relevant PSM Elements
docs.text:
Process Safety Information (PSI): PSM requires complete documentation of the process: P&IDs, equipment data, valve data sheets, safety system descriptions. Applied Control's role: maintain valve data sheets with correct specifications; provide DVC6200 configuration records.

Mechanical Integrity (MI): PSM requires documented inspection, testing, and maintenance of equipment in covered processes. For pressure relief valves: test intervals, as-found data, repair records, and certification must be maintained. Applied Control's valve shop provides the test certificates that satisfy PSM MI documentation for PRVs.

Management of Change (MOC): Any change to process equipment (including valves) in a PSM-covered facility requires formal change review before implementation. Applied Control should notify customers when recommending valve trim changes or positioner configuration changes — these are MOC-triggering changes in PSM plants.

Pre-Startup Safety Review (PSSR): New or modified equipment requires a safety review before startup. Documentation of valve configuration, DVC6200 baseline signature, and PRV certification is part of the PSSR package.

docs.title: 15.7 ATEX and Hazardous Area Classification
docs.text:
Process plants have hazardous areas — zones where flammable gases, vapors, or dusts may be present and where ignition sources (sparks, hot surfaces) could cause explosion. Electrical equipment in these zones must be certified for the hazardous area classification.

NEC (US) classification system:

Class Hazard Class I Flammable gases or vapors Class II Combustible dusts Class III Ignitable fibers

Division system:

Division Hazard present Division 1 Under normal operating conditions Division 2 Only under abnormal conditions (failure, maintenance)

IEC/ATEX (International) zone system:

Zone Gas/vapor Zone 0 Continuously present Zone 1 Frequently present Zone 2 Occasionally present

Fisher DVC6200 certifications: - FM Explosionproof: Class I, Division 1 and 2 - ATEX II 2G (Zone 1): Ex d IIC T6 - CSA Explosionproof and Intrinsically Safe

When specifying a DVC6200 for a hazardous area, confirm the area classification and select the matching certification mark. The wrong certification can create an OSHA citation — the right certification protects the plant.

ANSI/FCI 70-2 defines leakage class. IEC 60534 governs control valve sizing. API 520/526 govern pressure relief valve sizing and dimensions. IEC 61511 is the safety lifecycle standard for SIS — driving SIL requirements, logic solver selection, and proof test frequency. docs.title: Upstream Oil & Gas — Wellhead and Gathering
docs.text:
Upstream production begins at the wellhead where produced fluids (oil, gas, water, sand) flow under reservoir pressure. Control valves in upstream service face the harshest conditions in any industry.

Wellhead choke valves: - Pressure: 3,000–15,000 PSIG wellhead shut-in pressure - Fluid: Mixed phase — gas, oil, and produced water with sand and solids - Challenge: Sand erosion destroys standard trim; high ΔP causes severe cavitation in liquid-heavy streams and high-velocity noise in gas-heavy streams - Solution: Fisher severe service choke valves with tungsten carbide or ceramic trim; staged pressure reduction for liquid service (Cavitrol); bean-type orifice for gas wells

Production separator control: - Level control on three-phase separators (oil/water/gas) - Fisher V150 Vee-Ball for oil and water leg control (handles produced water solids) - Fisher EZ or ED for gas back-pressure control - Rosemount 5302 GWR for oil/water interface level

Flow measurement: - Rosemount 3051 with orifice plate or Annubar: gas and liquid well test measurement - Micro Motion Coriolis: custody transfer measurement at lease automatic custody transfer (LACT) units - Rosemount 8800D: flare gas measurement for environmental reporting

docs.title: Midstream — Gas Processing
docs.text:
Natural gas processing plants remove liquids (NGLs — ethane, propane, butane) and impurities (CO₂, H₂S) from the gas stream before pipeline transmission.

Key applications: - Amine absorber/regenerator (acid gas removal): Control valves handling hot amine (H₂S-containing); pitting corrosion from carbonic acid; Fisher D3 or ED with Hastelloy trim - Refrigeration/turboexpander: Anti-surge valve on compressor recycle; extremely fast-stroking (volume booster + DVC6200); Fisher ED with volume booster - NGL fractionation: Depropanizer, deethanizer, debutanizer column control; Fisher HP or ED; column differential pressure for tray efficiency

Measurement: - Chromatography (GC): Composition measurement for BTU content and custody transfer quality - Coriolis: Liquid NGL custody transfer at truck/rail loading racks - Vortex (8800D): Plant fuel gas metering

docs.title: 16.2 Petroleum Refining
docs.text: A refinery is the highest-density concentration of critical control valve service in any industry. A mid-size 200,000 BPD refinery may contain 2,000–5,000 control valves; a significant percentage are severe service.

docs.title: Crude Distillation Unit (CDU)
docs.text:
The CDU separates crude oil into fractions by boiling point. It is the most important unit in the refinery — a CDU shutdown stops the entire plant.

Key CDU control valve applications:

Application Service challenge Fisher solution Atmospheric column overhead Corrosive HCl/H₂O condensate; erosion from naphthas Fisher HP with Hastelloy C wetted parts; PTFE packing Atmospheric column bottoms High temperature (650°F+); high viscosity; coking Fisher HP-20 high-temp design; insulating extension bonnet Crude charge heater fuel gas Combustion safety (fail-closed); fast response Fisher EZ with 667 (fail-closed) and DVC6200 PST Atmospheric column side streams Moderate service; high cycle frequency Fisher ED with DVC6200 Vacuum column overhead Very low pressure (vacuum); large flow capacity; condensables Fisher ET or HP with large Cv; special vacuum trim

docs.title: Fluid Catalytic Cracking (FCC)
docs.text:
FCC converts heavy gas oils into more valuable gasoline and diesel using a fluidized catalyst system at 900–1100°F.

Severe service challenges: - Catalyst carryover in gas streams creates severe erosion - High temperature requires exotic metallurgy - Flue gas from catalyst regenerator: high-temperature, corrosive, particulate-laden

Fisher solutions for FCC: - Slide gate valves (Fisher proprietary) for catalyst circulation — standard globe valves cannot handle catalyst-laden flow - High-temperature HP valves with Stellite-faced trim for erosive service - WhisperFlo cage trim for flue gas noise control

docs.title: Hydroprocessing (Hydrotreater, Hydrocracker)
docs.text:
Hydrotreating removes sulfur, nitrogen, and metals from distillate streams using high-pressure hydrogen (500–2500 PSIG) at elevated temperature (500–800°F).

Critical considerations: - Hydrogen embrittlement: Carbon steel fails in hydrogen service above 300°F — Nelson curves (API 941) define the allowable temperature/pressure combinations for each steel alloy. Chrome-moly (1.25 Cr, 2.25 Cr) is required for high-temperature hydrogen service. - HTHA (High Temperature Hydrogen Attack): Hydrogen reacts with carbides in carbon steel at elevated temperature, weakening the steel. Fisher HP and specialty valves use appropriate Cr-Mo alloys for hydroprocessing service. - High pressure: Class 1500–2500 valves; Fisher HP series covers these classes

docs.title: Power Generation — Thermal Power Plants
docs.text:
Coal-fired and gas-fired power plants are among Applied Control's most important customers because of the critical nature of the control functions involved.

Steam turbine control: - HP and IP turbine admission/control valves: High-pressure, high-temperature steam (1050°F, 2400 PSIG in supercritical plants); Class 2500 Fisher EHD valves - Turbine bypass: Routes steam directly to condenser during load rejection; must stroke fully in < 2 seconds; Fisher HP with volume booster - Reheat stop valve: Safety isolation on reheated steam; Fisher HP with 667 fail-closed

Feedwater control: - Boiler feedwater control valve: The most critical valve in the plant — controls boiler drum level and feedwater flow at very high ΔP (900 PSIG typical); Class 600–1500 Fisher HP - Startup feedwater bypass: Small valve for low-flow startup control; Fisher ED

Combustion air and fuel gas: - Fuel gas control: Fail-closed (667); DVC6200 with partial stroke testing for SIL compliance - Combustion air dampers: Large-area modulating air control; butterfly valves with electric actuators

Emissions control: - SCR (Selective Catalytic Reduction) ammonia injection: Precise NH₃ dosing for NOₓ control; Fisher ED or EZ with Rosemount flow measurement - FGD (Flue Gas Desulfurization) slurry control: Abrasive limestone slurry; Fisher Vee-Ball or eccentric plug valves

Key Applied Control message for power: "Every MW of generation lost to a valve-caused trip costs dispatch revenue. Our DVC6200 diagnostic program prevents the valve trips that cost you generation."

docs.title: Ethylene Cracking Furnace
docs.text:
Ethylene is produced by thermal cracking of naphtha or ethane in radiant furnace tubes at 1400–1600°F. The furnace outlet quench system requires very fast-acting, high-temperature valves.

Transfer line exchangers (TLE) isolation: Must close within 0.5 seconds on furnace trip; Fisher Y-design 3-way valves; volume boosters for fast stroke; tight shutoff required.

Furnace feed control: - Naphtha/steam feed: Flow ratio control; Fisher ED with DVC6200 - Steam dilution: Precise steam-to-hydrocarbon ratio; Fisher EZ or ED

docs.title: Distillation Column Control
docs.text:
Distillation is the workhorse separation process in petrochemicals. A typical large distillation column has:

  • Overhead condenser control: Reflux flow, overhead product, vent; Fisher ED
  • Reboiler duty control: Steam to reboiler; Fisher EZ or ED (fail-closed on steam)
  • Feed preheat: Feed temperature; Fisher EZ
  • Bottoms level: Column sump; Fisher Vee-Ball for high-viscosity or solids-containing bottoms
  • Column differential pressure: Rosemount 3051 ΔP for tray efficiency monitoring

Distillation cascade control in DeltaV: Composition control (analyzer feedback) → inferential temperature control → flow control cascade — a classic three-level cascade that DeltaV implements with HART integration from bottom to top.

docs.title: Reactor Temperature Control
docs.text:
Exothermic chemical reactors require precise temperature control — too cold = poor conversion; too hot = runaway reaction.

Cooling water jacket control: - Typical: One control valve on cooling water inlet (temperature feedback from reactor) - Advanced: Cascade — outer loop reactor temperature, inner loop coolant outlet temperature - Safety: High temperature → SIS activates emergency quench; DeltaV SIS with DVC6200 PST

Critical sizing: The cooling control valve must have sufficient Cv to handle emergency cooling loads — not just normal operating flow. Oversizing the valve too much creates throttling control issues; undersizing creates inability to cool during exotherms.

  • Apply: Specify the correct Fisher valve, actuator, and positioner for a WFI (Water for Injection) distribution loop that requires cGMP compliance and full electronic audit trail
  • Analyze: Compare the measurement and control requirements of a municipal water treatment plant to a pharmaceutical purified water system, and identify the key differences
  • Evaluate: Identify the three most important Applied Control differentiators for a pharmaceutical customer conducting a vendor qualification audit

docs.title: 17.1 Life Sciences — Pharmaceutical and Biotech
docs.text: Pharmaceutical and biotechnology manufacturing is among the most regulated industries in the world. Every piece of process equipment — including control valves and transmitters — must meet FDA requirements for hygiene, cleanability, and documentation.

docs.title: Regulatory Framework
docs.text:
FDA 21 CFR Part 11 — Electronic Records and Signatures: Any electronic record that substitutes for a paper record in a regulated process must meet 21 CFR Part 11 requirements: - Audit trail: Complete record of all configuration changes, calibration events, and alarm acknowledgments — with timestamp and user identity - Access control: Role-based access; operators cannot change valve configuration; only qualified engineers can - Data integrity: Records cannot be modified without creating a new record with the change documented

FDA 21 CFR Part 210/211 — Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP): cGMP defines the manufacturing practices required for drug product production. For process equipment: - Equipment must be designed and installed to facilitate cleaning and maintenance - Equipment qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ) must be documented before use in production - Calibration of all measuring instruments must be documented and traceable to NIST

The DeltaV + DVC6200 documentation advantage: DeltaV's historian records every process value, alarm, and operator action with timestamp — meeting 21 CFR Part 11 audit trail requirements. The DVC6200 records all configuration changes via HART audit trail in AMS Device Manager. This electronic documentation package significantly reduces the burden of paper-based batch record systems.

docs.title: Sanitary Design — 3-A Standards
docs.text:
3-A Sanitary Standards (defined by 3-A SSI — Sanitary Standards Inc.) specify design requirements for food, beverage, and dairy equipment that must be cleanable to microbiological standards:

  • No dead legs: All wetted surfaces must drain completely; no horizontal dead legs longer than 3× the pipe diameter
  • Surface finish: Wetted surfaces 32 Ra μin (0.8 μm Ra) or better — typically electropolished 316L stainless steel
  • No crevices: All connections use clamp-type tri-clamp (sanitary) connections — no threaded fittings with crevice corrosion sites
  • Drainability: All vessels and piping slope to drain; no puddles
  • Cleanability: Equipment must withstand CIP (Clean-in-Place) with hot caustic and hot acid; SIP (Steam-in-Place) at 121°C minimum for sterilization

Fisher sanitary valve offerings: - Fisher V-Series sanitary ball valves: 3-A certified, tri-clamp ends, electropolished 316L, EPDM or silicone seats, full-bore design - Fisher ES butterfly valve: Sanitary elastomer seat, tri-clamp, for large-bore low-pressure service - DVC6200 on sanitary valves: Standard DVC6200 with sanitary mount kit; HART audit trail meets 21 CFR Part 11

docs.title: Water for Injection (WFI) Systems
docs.text:
WFI is the highest-purity water used in pharmaceutical manufacturing — used for final product formulation, equipment rinsing, and injectables. WFI distribution loops typically circulate at 80°C or higher to prevent microbial growth.

WFI control requirements: - Temperature: 80–85°C maintained continuously (monitored by Rosemount RTDs at multiple points) - Flow: Minimum circulation velocity to prevent biofilm formation (>1 m/s) - Control valves: Sanitary design, zero dead legs, 316L electropolished, DVC6200 with HART audit

Point-of-use (POU) valves: At each process connection point, a diaphragm valve or sanitary ball valve controls WFI delivery. Fisher sanitary diaphragm valves (PTFE-lined body, EPDM diaphragm) are common for these applications.

docs.title: Equipment Qualification — IQ/OQ/PQ
docs.text:
Before a control valve or DCS can be used in FDA-regulated production, it must be qualified:

Phase Stands for What is documented IQ (Installation Qualification) Installation Qualification Valve model, tag, serial number, materials of construction, connection sizes match the design specification OQ (Operational Qualification) Operational Qualification Valve strokes correctly; DVC6200 calibration verified; HART communication confirmed; fail-safe action confirmed PQ (Performance Qualification) Performance Qualification The control loop performs within specification during production — temperature held within ±0.5°C, flow controlled within ±1%

Applied Control can prepare the IQ/OQ documentation package as part of a project delivery — a significant differentiator for pharmaceutical customers who spend enormous effort on qualification documentation.

docs.title: 17.2 Food and Beverage
docs.text:
Food and beverage manufacturing shares many requirements with pharmaceutical — sanitary design, CIP/SIP compatibility, FDA compliance — but with somewhat less stringent documentation requirements (no IQ/OQ/PQ for most food processes).

Key segments and Applied Control opportunities:

docs.title: Dairy
docs.text:
• Pasteurization control: Precise temperature control at 161°F/72°C (HTST) or 280°F/138°C (UHT); Fisher sanitary globe or butterfly valve; Rosemount temperature with sanitary tri-clamp connection
  • Cream separation: Centrifuge control; Rosemount magnetic flow for volume measurement
  • CIP systems: Caustic and acid cleaning solutions at high temperature; EPDM seats for caustic compatibility; silicone seats for acid compatibility

docs.title: Beverage (Beer, Soft Drinks, Juice)
docs.text:
• Carbonation control: CO₂ dosing; precise pressure control; Rosemount pressure transmitter; Fisher EZ or ED
  • Blending: Multi-stream ratio control; Micro Motion Coriolis for precise ingredient dosing by mass
  • Fermentation temperature: Glycol cooling control; Fisher EZ with 667 (fail-closed cooling = fail-open glycol) or 657 (fail-open cooling)

docs.title: Brewing — Unique Requirements
docs.text: Brewing involves biological processes (yeast fermentation) that are highly sensitive to temperature and oxygen exposure. DeltaV batch control is ideal for recipe-based brewing where each batch step (mash temperature ramp, yeast pitch temperature, fermentation temperature profile) is defined in a recipe and executed consistently across hundreds of batches.

docs.title: Municipal Water Treatment
docs.text:
Water treatment plants process raw surface water or groundwater into potable drinking water. Key process steps and Applied Control opportunities:

Coagulation and flocculation: - Chemical dosing (alum, polymer): Precise flow control; Rosemount magnetic flowmeter (Coriolis for smaller flows); Fisher EZ or EW globe valve - pH control: Rosemount pH transmitter; lime or CO₂ dosing valve

Filtration: - Filter backwash: High-flow, brief-duration valves; Fisher HP butterfly for large-bore backwash headers - Filter influent/effluent control: Butterfly valves with electric actuators (no instrument air in many water plants)

Disinfection: - Chlorination: Chlorine gas or sodium hypochlorite dosing; corrosion-resistant trim (Hastelloy or titanium wetted parts); Rosemount flow measurement - UV disinfection: No chemical dosing; simpler control

Distribution pump control: - Variable speed drives (VFDs) on main distribution pumps; Rosemount pressure transmitters for system pressure feedback; Fisher control valves on pressure zones and PRV stations

docs.title: Wastewater Treatment
docs.text:
Primary treatment (screening and settling): No significant control valve content.

Secondary treatment (biological — activated sludge): - Aeration control: Dissolved oxygen measurement (Rosemount optical DO sensor); modulating air blower VFD or butterfly valve to maintain DO at 2 mg/L setpoint - Return activated sludge (RAS) flow: Fisher V-notch Vee-Ball or eccentric plug valve (handles sludge solids) - Waste activated sludge (WAS): Fisher Vee-Ball; flow measurement by Rosemount magnetic meter

Sludge treatment (anaerobic digester): - Digester temperature: 95–100°F (mesophilic); heat exchanger with Fisher EZ temperature control - Biogas pressure: Self-regulating Fisher 627 regulator for biogas supply to boilers - Biogas flow: Thermal mass flowmeter (low pressure, variable composition)

Applied Control message for water/wastewater: "We understand the constraints — no instrument air at most sites, tight capital budgets, and operators who maintain equipment rather than instrumentation specialists. Fisher Vee-Balls with electric actuators, Rosemount instruments with WirelessHART where wiring is cost-prohibitive, and 627 self-contained regulators for pump stations — simple, reliable, and maintainable by your staff."

docs.title: 17.4 HVAC and Building Automation
docs.text:
HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning) is not Applied Control's core market, but represents opportunity in large industrial and campus facilities where central utility systems include steam, chilled water, and cooling tower control.

Central plant control: - Chilled water supply temperature: Centrifugal chiller control; large butterfly valves on evaporator and condenser water circuits - Steam-to-hot water heat exchangers: Fisher EZ globe valve with 667 actuator (fail-closed); steam pressure downstream of PRV (Fisher 627 regulator) for building heat - Cooling tower basin level: Makeup water control; Fisher EZ or EW globe valve; Rosemount level measurement

Differential pressure control for variable air volume (VAV) systems: - Building supply air pressure is maintained by variable-speed supply fans with duct static pressure feedback - Zone-level VAV boxes control individual zone temperatures with small butterfly or ball valves - Rosemount differential pressure transmitters (3051) monitor filter status and system balance

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: Life sciences manufacturing requires the highest level of documentation, hygienic design, and process control precision. Fisher sanitary valves (3-A compliant), DVC6200 with 21 CFR Part 11 audit trail, and DeltaV batch control provide the complete package for pharmaceutical and food/beverage applications. Water and wastewater treatment requires reliable, low-maintenance equipment tolerant of solids and variable flow conditions — Fisher Vee-Ball and eccentric plug valves for sludge; Rosemount magnetic meters for flow; WirelessHART for remote sites without wiring infrastructure; Fisher 627 regulators for pump station pressure control. docs.title: Glossary of Valve Automation Terms
docs.text:
This glossary covers key terms from the Applied Control Valve Automation Mastery textbook. Terms are defined following ISO 11179 metadata registry principles: each definition is precise, non-circular, and written from the perspective of a practitioner in valve automation and process control.

Use Ctrl+F (or the search icon in the navigation) to find any term quickly.

docs.title: A
docs.text:
Actuator A device that converts an energy source (pneumatic pressure, electrical current, hydraulic pressure) into mechanical motion to position a control valve. The actuator is the muscle of the control valve assembly.

AMS Device Manager Emerson's asset management software platform that collects diagnostic data from HART and FOUNDATION Fieldbus devices across a plant, provides alert management, and generates maintenance work orders. The primary tool for managing FIELDVUE DVC6200 positioner diagnostics.

ANSI Class (Pressure Class) A standardized pressure-temperature rating system defined by ASME B16.34 for valve body flanges. Classes include 150, 300, 600, 900, 1500, and 2500, with higher numbers indicating higher maximum allowable working pressures.

Anti-cavitation trim Valve trim designed to prevent cavitation by dropping pressure in multiple stages, keeping local pressure above vapor pressure throughout the flow path. The Fisher Cavitrol III is the standard anti-cavitation trim for Fisher ED and similar globe valve bodies.

Authority (valve) The ratio of valve pressure drop at full flow to total system pressure drop at full flow. High authority (β > 0.25) means the installed flow characteristic approximates the inherent characteristic.

docs.title: B
docs.text:
Back-pressure regulator A self-contained pressure control device that maintains a set pressure on its upstream side by venting or bypassing excess flow downstream.

Bernoulli's equation The energy conservation equation for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow stating that the sum of static pressure, dynamic pressure (½ρv²), and hydrostatic head is constant along a streamline. Foundational to understanding pressure profiles through control valves.

Body (valve) The primary pressure-containing element of a control valve, housing the trim, flow passages, and end connections. The body material and pressure class define the valve's operating envelope.

Bonnet The top closure of a globe valve body that houses the stem, packing, and (in extended-bonnet designs) an insulating column for high-temperature or cryogenic service.

Bubble-tight shutoff (Class VI) The highest leakage class per ANSI FCI 70-2. Achieves virtually zero leakage under test conditions. Requires soft seats (PTFE, elastomer) and is specified for toxic, cryogenic, or other critical isolation services.

Butterfly valve A quarter-turn valve using a disk rotating on a central shaft to control flow. Types include concentric (wafer), high-performance (double-offset), and triple-offset. Higher-offset designs provide better shutoff and throttling control.

docs.title: C
docs.text:
Cage A cylindrical trim component in globe valves that guides the plug, defines the flow characteristic through window openings, and can incorporate noise attenuation or anti-cavitation features. The Fisher ED uses cage-guided trim.

Cage-guided trim A valve trim design where the plug is centered and guided by the cage throughout its travel, providing excellent stability and precise positioning. Standard design in the Fisher ED control valve.

Cascade control A control architecture where the output of an outer (primary) controller sets the setpoint of an inner (secondary) controller. The inner loop is faster and rejects disturbances before they reach the outer loop.

Cavitation The formation and rapid collapse of vapor bubbles in a liquid when local pressure drops below vapor pressure and then recovers. Bubble collapse generates shock waves that erode valve trim and create broadband noise.

Cavitation index (sigma, σ) A dimensionless number quantifying cavitation risk: σ = (P₂ − Pᵥ)/ΔP. Lower values indicate greater cavitation severity. When σ falls below the inception sigma (σᵢ) for the valve, cavitation is occurring.

Cavitrol III Fisher's proprietary multi-stage anti-cavitation trim. Available in 2-stage and 3-stage configurations. Drops pressure incrementally to keep local pressure above vapor pressure through the entire flow path.

cGMP (Current Good Manufacturing Practice) FDA regulations governing pharmaceutical manufacturing, requiring validated processes, documented procedures, and electronic audit trails. Control valve diagnostics with FIELDVUE DVC6200 support cGMP compliance.

CHARM (Characterized I/O Module) Emerson's single-channel I/O card for DeltaV. CHARMs enable electronic marshalling — I/O type is configured in software, eliminating the need to pull a field wire when I/O assignment changes.

Choked flow The condition in which increasing differential pressure across a valve produces no additional flow. Occurs when the velocity at the vena contracta reaches the local speed of sound. Maximum flow is then a function of upstream conditions only.

CIS (Concept Impact Score) In the Applied Control learning graph, the CIS measures how many other concepts depend (directly or indirectly) on a given concept. High-CIS concepts are foundational — mastering them enables mastering many downstream topics. Calculated recursively: CIS(x) = 1 + Σ CIS(d).

Control valve A variable-orifice device that regulates fluid flow in a process control loop by varying the flow area through the valve. The final control element in a feedback control loop.

Controller output (CO) The signal generated by the controller and sent to the final element (valve). In a standard loop, 4–20 mA maps to 0–100% valve travel.

Cv (flow coefficient) The number of US gallons per minute of water (at 60°F) that flows through a valve at a pressure drop of 1 PSID. The universal sizing parameter for control valves.

docs.title: D
docs.text:
Dead time The time delay between a change in controller output (manipulated variable) and the first detectable response in the process variable. Dead time degrades control loop performance and reduces achievable closed-loop bandwidth.

DeltaV DCS Emerson's flagship Distributed Control System. Features CHARMs electronic marshalling, integrated HART diagnostics, built-in function block programming (IEC 61131-3), and native integration with FIELDVUE positioners and Rosemount transmitters.

DeltaV SIS Emerson's Safety Instrumented System logic solver, integrated with the DeltaV platform. IEC 61508-certified logic solver for Safety Instrumented Functions rated to SIL 2 and SIL 3.

Derivative (D) action Controller output contribution proportional to the rate of change of the error signal. Anticipates process movement and pre-corrects; amplifies sensor noise and is often set to zero for noisy measurements.

ΔP (differential pressure) The difference in pressure between upstream (P₁) and downstream (P₂) of a valve. ΔP drives flow; higher ΔP = higher flow for the same Cv.

DVC6200 (FIELDVUE Digital Valve Controller) Fisher's flagship intelligent positioner. Provides precise valve position control, HART communication, full valve signature, friction trending, travel deviation alerting, and partial stroke testing capability.

DVC2000 (FIELDVUE Digital Valve Controller) Fisher's entry-level smart positioner. Provides HART communication and basic diagnostics without full signature analysis capability.

docs.title: E
docs.text:
ED valve (Fisher) Fisher's most versatile general-purpose control valve. Single-port globe body, cage-guided trim, available in 1/2" to 20", ANSI 150 to 2500, with a full range of trim options including Cavitrol III and WhisperFlo.

Equal-percentage characteristic A flow characteristic in which equal increments of valve travel produce equal percentage increases in Cv. Formula: Cv = Cv_max × R^(t-1), where R is rangeability and t is fractional travel. Provides constant process gain across a wide flow range. Most common characteristic for throttling service.

Error signal In a feedback control loop, the difference between setpoint (SP) and process variable (PV): e = SP − PV. The controller drives error toward zero.

EZ valve (Fisher) A cost-optimized single-port globe valve with stem-guided trim for lower-pressure general service. Size range ¾" to 6", ANSI 150 to 300. Used where cage-guided precision is not required.

docs.title: F
docs.text:
Fail-safe action The valve position reached on loss of control signal or instrument air supply. Selection is based on process safety analysis: fail-open for cooling valves, fail-closed for fuel or feed valves.

FIELDVUE Fisher's brand name for intelligent valve controllers (positioners) with digital communication and diagnostic capabilities. The DVC6200 is the flagship FIELDVUE product.

FL (liquid pressure recovery factor) A dimensionless factor (0 to 1) characterizing how much pressure recovers between the vena contracta and the valve outlet. Higher FL means less pressure recovery, and more resistance to cavitation for a given service condition. Globe valves have higher FL (0.85–0.95) than ball valves (0.55–0.75).

Flashing A two-phase flow condition in which downstream pressure (P₂) is below vapor pressure (Pᵥ). Unlike cavitation, vapor bubbles formed at the vena contracta do not collapse but persist through the valve outlet as vapor phase.

Flow characteristic The relationship between valve travel and flow capacity (Cv). Inherent characteristics (linear, equal-percentage, quick-opening) describe lab behavior; installed characteristics describe actual process behavior accounting for system pressure changes with flow.

FOUNDATION Fieldbus A digital process communication protocol for process instrumentation. Provides bi-directional digital communication, distributed control with function blocks in field devices, and eliminates analog-to-digital conversion.

Function block In DeltaV and IEC 61131-3 programming, a reusable control algorithm module. Standard blocks include PID, AI (analog input), AO (analog output), and dozens of advanced control functions.

docs.title: G
docs.text: Globe valve A linear-motion valve with fluid flowing through a circular seat port, controlled by a plug or disk attached to a stem. The most common control valve style for throttling service. Named for the historically spherical body shape.

docs.title: H
docs.text:
HART protocol Highway Addressable Remote Transducer. A digital communication standard that rides on the standard 4–20 mA analog signal. HART allows configuration, calibration, diagnostics, and process variables to be read digitally without replacing the analog infrastructure.

High-performance butterfly valve (HPBV) A butterfly valve with a double-eccentric (double-offset) disk design that provides better shutoff (Class III–IV) and throttling range than concentric wafer butterflies. Fisher 8580 series.

HP series (Fisher) Fisher's high-pressure globe valve series. Available in ANSI 600 to 4500 pressure classes for severe service: high-pressure steam conditioning, gas letdown, supercritical service.

docs.title: I
docs.text:
IEC 60534 International standard for control valve flow capacity sizing. Defines sizing equations for liquid, gas, and steam service, including correction factors for viscosity, piping geometry, two-phase flow, and noise.

IEC 61508 International standard for functional safety of electrical/electronic/programmable electronic systems. Defines SIL levels and the safety lifecycle for safety-critical systems.

IEC 61511 International standard for functional safety of safety instrumented systems in the process industry. Defines SIL targets, LOPA methodology, and proof testing requirements. Specifies how IEC 61508-certified equipment (DeltaV SIS, DVC6200) is applied in process plants.

Integral (I) action Controller output contribution proportional to the accumulated error over time. Eliminates steady-state offset. Can cause integral windup if the valve saturates.

Instrument air Clean, dry, oil-free compressed air used to power pneumatic actuators and instruments. Typical plant supply: 80–120 PSIG; instrument headers: 18–35 PSIG.

Installed characteristic The actual relationship between valve travel and flow in a piping system, accounting for the fact that system pressure drop changes with flow rate. Differs from the inherent (lab-measured) characteristic unless valve authority is high.

docs.title: K
docs.text: Kv The metric equivalent of Cv: the flow rate in m³/h of water at 1 bar ΔP. Conversion: Cv = 1.156 × Kv. Used in IEC documents; Cv is used in ISA and Fisher sizing software.

docs.title: L
docs.text:
Leakage class A classification per ANSI FCI 70-2 defining the maximum allowable leak rate through a closed control valve. Classes range from Class I (no test required) to Class VI (bubble-tight). Fisher globe valves standard: Class IV (0.01% of rated Cv).

Linear characteristic A flow characteristic in which Cv is directly proportional to valve travel: Cv = Cv_max × t. Best when valve pressure drop is constant (high valve authority).

LOPA (Layer of Protection Analysis) A risk assessment method used to determine SIL targets. Each independent protection layer (IPL) reduces risk by a factor of 10–100. The required SIL is determined by how much risk reduction remains to be provided by the Safety Instrumented Function.

docs.title: M
docs.text:
Manipulated variable (MV) The process variable that the controller adjusts through the final element (valve) to bring the controlled variable to setpoint. In a level control loop, MV is typically the outlet flow rate.

Micro Motion Emerson's brand of Coriolis mass flow and density meters. Measures mass flow directly (not volumetrically) using the Coriolis effect on vibrating flow tubes. Used for custody transfer, batch control, and two-phase density measurement.

Multi-stage pressure drop A valve trim design philosophy in which the total pressure drop is divided across multiple stages, preventing any single stage from creating conditions for cavitation or excessive noise. Implemented in Cavitrol III, WhisperFlo, and similar Fisher trims.

docs.title: N
docs.text:
NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 The material requirement standard for equipment used in H₂S-containing (sour) service in oil and gas. Specifies maximum hardness limits and approved alloys to prevent sulfide stress cracking. Applied Control specifies NACE-compliant materials for sour service applications.

Noise attenuation trim Valve trim designed to reduce aerodynamic noise in gas or steam service by dividing the flow into many small-diameter jets, reducing jet velocity and noise generation. Fisher WhisperFlo and WhisperTrim are standard noise attenuation trims.

docs.title: P
docs.text:
Packing The sealing material around the valve stem that prevents process fluid from escaping to atmosphere. Common packing types: PTFE (low friction, chemical resistance), graphite (high temperature), live-loaded spring packing (low fugitive emissions, LDAR compliance).

Partial stroke test (PST) A safety valve proof test method in which the valve is moved a partial stroke (typically 10–15%) while remaining in service to verify mechanical integrity. Performed by the DVC6200 without requiring process shutdown. Required documentation for SIL 2/SIL 3 safety instrumented functions under IEC 61511.

PFDavg (Average Probability of Failure on Demand) The statistical measure used to determine SIL: the probability that a SIF will fail to respond when demanded. Lower PFDavg = higher SIL. Calculated from component failure rates, diagnostic coverage, and proof test intervals.

PID controller A feedback controller combining three modes: Proportional (present error), Integral (accumulated error), Derivative (rate of change of error). The most common control algorithm in industrial process control.

Plug The moving trim element in a globe valve that controls flow area by varying its position relative to the seat ring. The plug profile determines the flow characteristic in non-cage-guided designs.

Positioner A local feedback controller mounted on the valve actuator that compares commanded position to actual stem position and modulates actuating pressure to eliminate position error. Eliminates the effect of packing friction and supply pressure variation on valve position.

Process variable (PV) The measured quantity to be controlled in a control loop (e.g., temperature, pressure, flow, level).

Proportional (P) action Controller output contribution directly proportional to current error. Faster response than integral, but leaves a steady-state offset.

docs.title: Q
docs.text: Quick-opening characteristic A flow characteristic in which most Cv increase occurs at low travel positions. Formula: Cv ≈ Cv_max × √t. Best for on/off service where maximum flow is needed immediately on opening.

docs.title: R
docs.text:
Rangeability The ratio of maximum to minimum controllable Cv: R = Cv_max/Cv_min. Fisher ED globe: 50:1; Fisher Vee-Ball: 100:1; concentric butterfly: 10:1.

Regulator (self-contained) A pressure control device that uses the controlled pressure to directly actuate the valve without requiring an external power source. Used for pressure reduction and back-pressure control at moderate accuracy requirements.

Reynolds number (Re) A dimensionless number characterizing flow regime: Re = ρvD/μ. Re < 2,000: laminar; Re > 4,000: turbulent. Standard Cv sizing tables assume turbulent flow; viscosity corrections are required for laminar or transitional service.

Rosemount Emerson's instrumentation brand. Key products: Rosemount 3051 pressure transmitter (the industry standard), Rosemount 8800 vortex flowmeter, Rosemount 5408 radar level transmitter, Rosemount 644 temperature transmitter.

docs.title: S
docs.text:
Safety Instrumented Function (SIF) A specific safety function that is implemented using a safety instrumented system (SIS). A SIF has a defined safe state, a demand rate, and a SIL target.

Safety Instrumented System (SIS) An instrumented system designed to bring a process to a safe state when predetermined conditions are violated. Consists of sensors, logic solver, and final elements (valves). Must be designed and maintained to IEC 61511 requirements.

Safety Integrity Level (SIL) A discrete level (1, 2, 3, or 4) corresponding to a range of safety integrity for a safety function. SIL 1 (PFDavg 0.1–0.01) through SIL 4 (PFDavg 0.0001–0.00001). Most process industry applications target SIL 2 or SIL 3.

Seat (valve) The fixed trim surface against which the plug seals when the valve is closed. Seat material affects leakage class, temperature rating, and corrosion resistance.

Setpoint (SP) The desired value of the process variable. Set by the operator or an outer control loop in cascade control.

SIL (see Safety Integrity Level)

Sigma (see Cavitation Index)

docs.title: T
docs.text:
TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) The lifetime cost of an asset including purchase, installation, maintenance, unplanned downtime, energy, and end-of-life. TCO analysis typically favors Fisher/Applied Control over lower-cost alternatives when unplanned downtime cost is included.

Throttling service Valve service in which the valve is required to modulate flow continuously at positions between fully closed and fully open. Requires stable, predictable flow characteristics and resistance to wear.

Trim The internal components of a control valve that are wetted by the process fluid and determine flow capacity, characteristic, shutoff, noise, and cavitation behavior: plug, seat ring, cage, stem.

Triple-offset butterfly valve A butterfly valve with three geometric offsets that create a cone-shaped seating geometry, eliminating friction during opening and closing. Achieves Class V/VI shutoff and is suitable for high-pressure, high-temperature service.

docs.title: V
docs.text:
Valve authority (see Authority)

Valve signature The stroke-by-stroke record of actuating pressure vs. stem travel (or vice versa) produced by a FIELDVUE DVC6200 during a stroke test. The signature reveals packing friction (hysteresis band width), seat condition, spring rate, and actuator health.

ValveLink Emerson's valve sizing and management software. Performs Cv sizing per IEC 60534, noise calculations per IEC 60534-8, cavitation analysis, actuator sizing, and generates sizing reports. Integrates with FIELDVUE diagnostics.

Vapor pressure (Pᵥ) The pressure at which a liquid begins to vaporize at a given temperature. When valve pressure drops below vapor pressure, cavitation (if P₂ > Pᵥ) or flashing (if P₂ < Pᵥ) occurs.

Vee-Ball (Fisher) Fisher's V-notch segmented ball valve series. The V-notch creates an inherent equal-percentage characteristic. Excellent for slurry, solids-laden, and large-flow liquid service. Rangeability 100:1.

Vena contracta The cross-sectional point of minimum flow area (and maximum velocity/minimum pressure) downstream of a valve orifice. Pressure at the vena contracta determines whether cavitation or flashing will occur.

docs.title: W
docs.text:
WhisperFlo / WhisperTrim Fisher's noise attenuation trim family for gas and steam service. Multiple small orifices divide a single high-velocity jet into many small jets, dramatically reducing aerodynamic noise per IEC 60534-8-3.

WirelessHART A wireless mesh network protocol for process instrumentation (IEC 62591). Built on HART application layer; enables installation of transmitters without wiring. Emerson Smart Wireless products include the 702/wireless THUM adapter.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Valve Automation Knowledge Map
docs.text:
The Learning Graph is the brain of this textbook. It maps all 490 concepts in the Applied Control curriculum as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) — each node is a concept, each edge represents a prerequisite dependency. Before you can truly understand a concept, you need its prerequisites.

This structure, pioneered by Dan McCreary's ibook-skills methodology, gives you something a traditional table of contents cannot: a knowledge topology that shows what to learn first, what unlocks what, and which concepts are the most foundational.

docs.title: How to Use This Graph
docs.text:
• Node size reflects the Concept Impact Score (CIS) — how many downstream concepts depend on this one. Large nodes are the most foundational.
  • Node color reflects the taxonomy category (see legend).
  • Click a node to see its definition, prerequisites, and what it unlocks.
  • Use the search box to find any concept by name.
  • Filter by category using the legend buttons.
  • Drag and zoom to explore the full graph.

Start here if you're new

The highest-CIS concepts — Fluid Mechanics (CIS=7143), Pressure (CIS=5031), Bernoulli Equation (CIS=2170) — are the foundation of everything. Chapter 1 and 2 cover these first.

docs.title: CIS — Concept Impact Score
docs.text:
The Concept Impact Score is computed using a PageRank-style recursion across the dependency graph:

CIS(x) = 1 + Σ CIS(d) for all direct dependents of x

A high CIS means that understanding this concept unlocks a large portion of the curriculum. The top 10 are the concepts every Applied Control sales engineer must master first.
